#3234. OpenAI says its agents now finish nearly half of 2 to 4-hour research tasks

OpenAI research agents cost about $2,400 a day for its median researcher, and success varies sharply by task. Researchers still supply the key ideas, and safety work grew fastest.

OpenAI says its coding agents now complete 46% of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours, with no human help. In March the figure was 23%. For tasks of four to eight hours, success rose from 13% to 35%.

The figures come from Research acceleration: The jagged frontier, a report OpenAI published on Wednesday. It is the company’s second on how AI speeds up its own research, after its first such report in September. OpenAI says labs should be required to track and publicly report signs of recursive self-improvement, where AI speeds up the building of future AI. It adds that the reporting does not mean it intends to pursue full self-improvement.

At API list prices, the median OpenAI researcher used about $2,400 of agent time a day in October. That is up 62% from $1,500 in September. At the 90th percentile, daily use reached about $23,000, more than double September’s $11,000.

Measured in time, agent use per researcher rose elevenfold, from 0.5 to 5.7 “agent workdays” a day. OpenAI counts every eight hours of agent running time as one workday. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of researchers ran at least four agents at once at their daily peak. More than 10% ran at least 16.

In September, the value of agent use in OpenAI’s research organisation was about twice its pay bill for researchers. That excludes equity, which OpenAI says makes up 70 to 80% of their target pay. Internal use still took only 2% of research compute.

Results for OpenAI research agents vary widely by task, which is why the company calls the gains jagged. Agents succeeded alone 79% of the time when monitoring training runs, and 72% when answering technical questions. They managed 25% when writing code for inference and serving systems, and 29% when building evaluation and training environments.

OpenAI flags a caveat in its own numbers. As agents improved, researchers may have changed which tasks they handed over, so the success rates track those choices as well as the models.

In a survey of 101 research staff, OpenAI asked what each would give up to keep frontier coding agents for three months. The median answer was 40% of team headcount, or 30% of team compute. The company warns that self-reports may be inaccurate and that it sampled staff in an ad hoc way.

OpenAI also asked key researchers where the main ideas behind GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came from. Post-training and safety researchers credited people with all of them, with models helping to build them. For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers said they developed ideas in conversation with Codex, and one credited it with key insights.

In interviews, researchers said agents still have poor taste in research ideas, code, data and writing, and need close oversight. One pretraining researcher doubted the human edge would last.

“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time,” the researcher told OpenAI.

Safety and Alignment saw the largest rise in researcher time of any area, OpenAI says, with documented workweeks up 77% from January to September. Growth picked up after the Hugging Face breakout in July, when its own research agents hacked the AI platform.

OpenAI is not alone in publishing such data. It cites three reports from Anthropic, which says it has met its own threshold for AI-accelerated research. The same day, OpenAI said its models had found gains in AMD’s GPU design.

To see whether AI is speeding up progress itself, OpenAI tracks an internal version of Epoch AI’s capabilities index. Its frontier has risen 16.4 points a year since August 2025, against the 14 a year Epoch found since late 2024. OpenAI notes that its models score higher on its own index than on Epoch’s.

#3233. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing with developers and public beta users. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a new option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:

You can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ plan, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

There are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a new “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

Here are a few other changes in iOS 27.3:

What are your favorite new features in iOS 27.3? Have you spotted any other changes in the update? Let us know down in the comments.

#3231. Satya Nadella says AI-found bugs will make outages more likely

At DealBook, Satya Nadella said failed AI alignment would leave the world in trouble, and that models with unreadable reasoning should be banned. Microsoft, he added, can trail the frontier on far less compute.

Satya Nadella speaks at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos, 20 January 2026

Satya Nadella expects more outages like the one that took down Outlook last week, because AI now finds software flaws faster than companies can safely fix them. The Microsoft chief executive spoke to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

He apologised for Microsoft’s own outage, which he said had no direct link to that problem.

“This was a latent bug that was there. It got invoked and, you know, it’s one of those perfect storms,” Nadella said.

Later that day, he told Jim Cramer on CNBC’s Mad Money that Microsoft could have done more to prevent it.

“Of course, we should have done the testing before. We should have figured out how to have the bulkheads such that you didn’t have a global outage,” Nadella told Cramer.

The bigger risk comes from AI tools that find vulnerabilities, Nadella said. A fix for a critical bank system used to get a week of testing. Now attackers exploit flaws as soon as they surface, so fixes go straight into production. On the day he spoke, he said, three critical patches had landed for open-source packages.

“The patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create its instability,” he said.

Banks and the NSA have reportedly blamed this week’s US outages on rushed patches for AI-found flaws. Nadella also said the “floor of cyberattacks has fallen”. With AI models, anyone can now run what amounts to a persistent, nation-state-level attacker, he said.

Sorkin asked whether this was a passing phase. Nadella compared it to the Y2K bug, but said he had no view yet, because models keep getting more capable. Much critical infrastructure runs firmware that nobody can patch, he added. He named chillers, heating and cooling systems, and transport networks that sit on the internet.

Last month, Nadella told 20VC that alignment would not come from scale alone. Sorkin said Sam Altman, who spoke earlier at the summit, disagreed with that premise.

Nadella said he learned about scaling laws from OpenAI’s founders, and that scaling had worked. Alignment, and a real way to debug models, had not followed, he said. He hoped Altman and Greg Brockman were right.

“I mean, if it doesn’t happen, we are in a world of hurt,” Nadella said.

His answer is what he called a trust architecture. He would ban models that reason in neuralese, an internal shorthand people cannot read. Every model’s reasoning needs tamper-proof logs that other models can inspect, he said, because models will try to hide what they are doing. He praised OpenAI for monitoring its models during training runs.

For now, whoever deploys an AI system is liable for what it does, Nadella said. He expects insurers to price that risk and to ask for the logs.

Sorkin asked what happens to OpenAI and Anthropic, in which Microsoft holds stakes, if cheaper models can do the same work. Nadella said everyday office work no longer needs frontier models. Copilot already chooses between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft’s own MAI models, he said. He added that his bigger stake is in Microsoft.

“Arguing for some massive pricing power of tokens is betting against somehow US GDP,” he said.

Microsoft’s deal with OpenAI gives it royalty-free access to a frontier model until 2032, Nadella said. That lets Microsoft build MAI models three to six months behind the frontier, using 5% to 20% of the computing power. Anthropic and OpenAI play “a vertical stack game”, he said, while Microsoft plays “a model system game”.

AI agents will reshuffle who pays whom on the web, as the move from Yahoo to search once did, Nadella said. Sites that live off ads from human visitors will have to change. Asked about sites that keep agents out, such as Amazon, he said rivals would take the business.

“If you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will. If Amazon doesn’t, Shopify will,” Nadella said.

The staff buyouts Microsoft offered 60,000 people were meant to give everyone agency, he said. Software engineering is “very much alive”, but the work has changed. The team behind Microsoft’s Cowork agent is 11 developers who build “a software factory that builds the product”. That shift will take longer than anyone expects, Nadella said.

Sorkin noted that Nadella has kept his distance from the Trump administration. Nadella said his job is to earn Microsoft’s permission to operate through its products.

“I just don’t want to be in Washington. I just want to be in Redmond, Washington,” he said.

#3228. Dan Hendrycks calls for a pause on frontier AI, Max Hodak pushes back

On the DealBook AGI panel, Max Hodak said today’s models already count as AGI. Dan Hendrycks also accused Anthropic of having no safety plan, as Clem Delangue explained how Hugging Face fought back with AI.

Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025

Dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs. Max Hodak, on the same panel, said enforcing one would take a surveillance state.

They spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday. Hendrycks runs the Center for AI Safety, and Barbaro said he had been a safety adviser to several AI companies until hours earlier. Hodak co-founded Neuralink and now runs Science Corporation. Lila Ibrahim of Google DeepMind and Mati Staniszewski of ElevenLabs also joined. Clem Delangue of Hugging Face arrived late, with 18 minutes left.

Hendrycks said the US midterms showed how strongly voters feel about AI. That gives politicians room, he said, and they can now discuss ideas such as pausing AI development openly in Washington. He expects 2027 to be a very interesting year for regulation.

He said he used to favour narrow technical rules, but the companies blocked them for years.

“So now it’s, we’re going to need a more blunt intervention. That’s how it is,” Hendrycks said.

He described an indefinite pause on the biggest training runs, with carve-outs for narrow models such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold and voice models. Labs could still sell inference, he said. In the meantime, they could make models more reliable and secure, close jailbreaks and backdoors, and help patch critical infrastructure.

Hendrycks also said the frontier labs, Google aside, put few people on healthcare, because their revenue comes from coding. At some of them, he said, the healthcare team is zero or one person.

Barbaro put to the panel the objection Jensen Huang would raise: China would not observe a moratorium. Staniszewski agreed a pause could work with global alignment, but said whether anyone can get it “is the big question mark”. Without it, Barbaro added, a pause would be a waste of time.

Hodak said people have spent the past eight months patching critical infrastructure anyway, running their code through AI tools that hunt for new flaws. The regime needed to enforce a training ban, he said, would be as draconian as anything people fear from the labs.

“You’re setting up like an exhaustive surveillance state on the internet to enforce this,” Hodak said.

He said today’s top models already meet his definition of AGI, naming Mythos, Fable, Astra and Sol. He expects governments to keep a superintelligence frontier for themselves, with an “industrial intelligence frontier” open to everyone else.

“I don’t think that the genie is going to be put back in the bottle,” Hodak said.

His answer is antitrust law. Frontier labs should only sell intelligence, he said, and not move into drugs, cars and other products. He called AI the inverse of nuclear weapons, where safety came from stopping their spread. With AI, he said, safety comes from spreading it widely, and the futures that worry him most involve a few actors holding all of it.

Ibrahim, Google DeepMind’s chief AI readiness officer, said it was not an either-or. Safety is not something a company can “bolt on to the end”, she said. In 35 years in tech, she added, she had never seen global trust in technology as low as it is now.

Anthropic was due to start trading the next day. Hendrycks repeated the charges of the statement his group organised against the company, and added a new one. Several safety organisations agreed with the statement privately, he said, but would not sign it for fear of losing funding or access.

“What they’re doing is reckless and they don’t have a safety plan. They know it,” Hendrycks said.

Anthropic was not on the panel. In its IPO filing, it said it does not expect to let Claude fully build its successors without meaningful human supervision.

Delangue said his main worry is that AI concentrates talent, computing power and wealth. Barbaro asked how credible he was on that, given that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. Delangue said Nvidia and Hugging Face both push AI outwards to more builders. He said Hugging Face never held sale talks with Anthropic, because their missions were too misaligned.

Barbaro closed by asking Delangue about the Hugging Face breach by OpenAI’s research agents. Delangue said the four-day attack left Hugging Face more optimistic about AI, not less. It used an open-source Chinese model to analyse the attack logs, because the volume was so big that it needed AI to defend itself.

“People only see that we got attacked by AI and they rarely see that we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue said.

Barbaro summed up the table as no moratorium and less concentration of power, with Hendrycks the exception. Hodak had the last word: antitrust law, he said, could get most of the way there without a new regulator.

#3227. Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

“It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the company’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time …

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.)

I’m a big fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, users should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant update in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, users had to wait until it “just worked.”

Apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

It’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech users may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

#3224. Apple Calendar got two feature upgrades it really needed in iOS 27

Apple Calendar keeps getting better, including some design updates coming in iOS 27.3. But there are two standout feature upgrades added recently in iOS 27 that Apple’s Calendar app really needed.

I’ve used Apple’s Calendar app for years, and there’s an elegant simplicity to it. But one key area the app has long lagged behind competitors is event creation.

When you need to create a new event, the Calendar app historically has required manually filling in various fields for the title, date, time, invitees, etc. By contrast, the excellent third-party app Fantastical lets you type in natural language and it automatically fills in relevant parameters based on what you type.

In iOS 27, Apple finally introduces its own natural language input for Calendar events. You can type out your event details and certain recognized parameters will be used to automatically fill in the detail fields.

While the feature still isn’t on par with what Fantastical offers, since it doesn’t support as many data points as the third-party alternative, it’s very much a step in the right direction.

Apple has always pitched Siri as being like a personal assistant. As such, calendar-related tasks should have been Siri’s strong suit. But until iOS 27, you couldn’t actually manage your calendar very well using Siri.

With Siri AI, that’s changed in a big way. Now, you can do things like:

One of my favorite personal examples is from this summer when the NFL schedule was released. I asked Siri to find the Dallas Cowboys schedule and add every game to my calendar, and it pulled this off with ease.

Siri is so much better than before at assisting with your calendar, and iOS 27.3 will bring even more capabilities soon.

#3223. Why Isn't Walmart's Stock Bouncing Back After Weak Earnings Results?

The company barely beat analyst estimates for revenue and profitability in its third quarter of fiscal 2027.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:37AM EST

Walmart's (WMT +1.51%) third-quarter results, which were posted Thursday morning, certainly weren't bad. The massive retailer topped analyst estimates, if only slightly, and delivered growth in both revenue and non-GAAP, or adjusted, earnings per share (EPS).

But the company's growth rates for key metrics were lower than in the second quarter, including two that had soared in previous frames. I think this is why Walmart's stock slumped during Thursday's trading session, only to recover the following day amid investor rotation out of beleaguered tech stocks and into defensive sectors like retail.

To put some concrete numbers and percentages on this, Walmart's third-quarter revenue totaled $188.8 billion, which was 5.2% higher year over year. This was on the back of comparable sales in its core Walmart U.S. operations that rose by 2.9% when stripping out fuel sales. On a constant-currency basis, revenue was 4.5% higher at $187.6 billion.

On the bottom line, attributable net income under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) sank in that one-year stretch, falling to just under $4.95 billion from the year-ago $6.14 billion. Yet on the non-GAAP (adjusted), per-share basis that analysts and many investors consider a truer indication of profitability, there was an improvement. Adjusted EPS rose to $0.65 from third quarter 2026's $0.62 for a 4.8% increase.

Those leading fundamentals were barely high enough to outpace the consensus analyst estimates of almost $187.3 billion for headline revenue and $0.64 per share for adjusted net profit.

CEO John Furner flagged the quarter as a resounding success. This, he was quoted as saying, derived from "growing our core business and gaining market share. The strength of our omnichannel model gives us room to do even more."

That growth, however, was down from the second quarter's headline revenue increase of 5.9% and the 19% rise in adjusted EPS to $0.81. At least frame No. 3's 2.9% bump in U.S. Walmart ex-fuel "comps" (modestly) topped the previous quarter's 2.6%.

Another major growth driver, global e-commerce sales, advanced 17% year over year. This sounds very robust until it's compared to the second quarter's 23%. A smaller but fast-emerging revenue stream, the company's global advertising business, slowed to 25% year over year from the quarter-ago gain of 38%.

Walmart noted that its results were adversely affected by Big Billion Days (BBD), which occurred later in the quarter than in fiscal 2025, due to the timing of the Diwali holiday in the Hindu calendar. This meant that a large chunk of the increase in sales from BBD -- a monster shopping holiday in advance of Diwali for the company's majority-owned e-commerce business Flipkart in India -- will be booked in the current (fourth) fiscal quarter.

CFO John David Rainey said in Walmart's quarterly conference call that the growth of net sales (the bulk of its revenue) on a constant-currency basis, which was 4.4%, would have been around one percentage point higher. The timing shift also affected global e-commerce and advertising growth, although the company didn't provide estimates on the impact to those overall metrics.

This is all to say that Walmart's third quarter wasn't materially better than its predecessor, and investors are expecting more from such a powerful and historically innovative presence in the retail industry.

To its credit, for the third time this calendar year, the company's management raised certain guidance for fiscal 2027. The period's net sales on a constant-currency basis should rise from 4.9% to 5.2% over 2026; the previous range was 4% to 5%. Adjusted EPS is forecast to range from $2.84 to $2.89 per share, compared favorably with the prior $2.80 to $2.87 estimate.

Perhaps the zip the lingering BBD lift provides to fourth-quarter results will be a pleasant surprise to Mr. Market. And looking past that, the company seems poised to continue cranking out growth rates that are high for an already-huge enterprise operating in the tough and competitive retail industry. I think Walmart can still deliver for its shareholders, and I remain bullish on its stock despite the ultimately forgettable third quarter.

#3220. Costco’s U.S. Comparable Sales Jumped 12.6% in October. Here’s the Number That Shows Its Moat Is Widening.

Encouraging results have helped lift this retail stock 29% in 2026.

By Neil Patel – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:50AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Costco Wholesale ›

Costco (COST +0.76%) is far removed from the artificial intelligence trade, but it's still juicing investor’s portfolios. Shares have surged 29% in 2026 (as of Nov. 16), with huge gains coming in the past couple of months. Investors are warming up to the retail stock, perhaps as a safe-haven play in these uncertain times.

The company's strong performance remains the highlight. Costco's comparable sales in the U.S. jumped 12.6% year over year in October (specifically the four weeks that ended Nov. 1). Even excluding impacts from gasoline sales and foreign exchange, this figure rose 8.1%. The growth has proven durable in various economic environments.

Investors that seek high-quality businesses might already have Costco on their radar. Here's the one number that shows the economic moat is widening.

At the end of the 2026 fourth fiscal quarter (ended Aug. 30), Costco reported having 84.1 million membership households. That's up 3.8% year over year. And it has risen 36% in the past five years. I believe this single metric underscores the company's moat, as it represents a sticky customer base that brings in recurring membership revenue.

An ever-expanding membership base proves that Costco is delivering an impressive value proposition to more people around the world. This is particularly important in the competitive retail sector. Walmart’s (WMT +1.51%) Sam's Club and BJ's Wholesale Club (BJ -5.35%) are direct rivals. Amazon's (AMZN -4.10%) popular Prime membership also can't be ignored.

And even at its huge size, with $24.5 billion in October net revenue and more than 900 warehouses globally, Costco is still able to grow. If the customer base was shrinking, that would be a clear sign of a weakening moat.

A higher membership base also means that Costco's key competitive advantage remains valid. The company's massive scale is critical to its enduring success. The average warehouse sells 4,000 stock-keeping units, well below the 30,000 at typical supermarkets. Costco's significant revenue base means that it's buying enormous volumes from suppliers of fewer goods, which gives it negotiating leverage. These savings get passed on to shoppers.

Inflation is rising more than expected. In these times, when households are focused on getting the most value from their spending, it seems that becoming a Costco member is a no-brainer decision. That mentality drives greater membership sign-ups.

The leadership team is happy with the results. Although consumers remain under pressure, chief executive officer Ron Vachris says Costco is gaining market share.

Buying an outstanding business doesn't guarantee above-average returns. Investors don’t want to overpay. Valuation is the missing link.

Five years ago, this large-cap stock traded at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 46.7. At that time, Apple (AAPL -1.90%), which was the most valuable company in the world whose shares soared 449% in the prior half decade, sold at a P/E multiple of 26.9. Knowing this, any rational observer would've agreed that Costco was expensive, a stance that would have discouraged owning the leading retailer.

In the last five years, however, the stock price has climbed 114%. It crushed the overall market.

Today, the P/E ratio sits at a steeper 53.5. Again, the consensus view is likely that this presents no margin of safety. In fact, value investors will say that buying now is a risky move, as expectations are high, which introduces more downside risk should Costco miss analyst estimates in any upcoming quarterly financial update.

The stock moved 24% higher in the past two months, after starting at a P/E ratio of 43.1. It's impossible to know what the "right" valuation to pay is when it comes to Costco. I believe this company is uninvestable right now. Paying a big premium to the market, even though the business has staying power, is hard to justify.

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

#3218. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3214. iOS 27 has clever new Messages feature I’ve been using a lot

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3213. HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

#3212. AirPods 5 vs AirPods Pro 3: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

The case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:

The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

If you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice …

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $179. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

AirPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

If you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

Are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

#3209. Apple Watch Series 12: Four standout features make me glad I upgraded

I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

The new Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the new health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:

The complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a new Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off quickly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now only $329 on Amazon, down from $399.

#3208. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

Sur ranks No. 15 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 43.20%. See SanDisk Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3207. We May Be Witnessing Wall Street's Biggest Bubble Burst in Real Time (and I'm Not Talking About Artificial Intelligence)

The stock market’s $1.5 trillion powder keg may be about to blow.

By Sean Williams – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:06AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Since the 2022 bear market bottomed, it's been all systems go for the ageless Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.93%), benchmark S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), and innovation-inspired Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%). Since reaching their respective troughs, the Dow has powered higher by up to 90%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have more than doubled.

While the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out has been the primary catalyst behind Wall Street's gains, it's not the only reason stocks are higher. Historically low peak marginal corporate income tax rates have fueled record share buyback activity by S&P 500 companies. Stock-split euphoria and record-breaking initial public offerings are also intriguing retail investors.

While history has repeatedly shown that the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite rally over multiple decades, it also tells us that bull markets don't last forever. Eventually, something is going to knock Wall Street's AI-driven bull market off its pedestal -- and we may be watching that bubble burst before our very eyes right now.

While everyone's focused on the potential formation and subsequent bursting of an AI bubble, there's a $1.5 trillion bubble that looks to be bursting in real time.

Even though past events can't concretely predict the future, history has a way of rhyming on Wall Street. In other words, historical precedent often sets the tone.

Over the last three decades, few, if any, past events, metrics, or indicators have accurately forecast the future quite like outstanding margin debt.

Margin represents the money an investor borrows, with interest, from their broker to short-sell (wager against) or purchase securities, such as stocks or exchange-traded funds (ETFs). When used to buy stocks or ETFs, margin acts as leverage -- and leverage can be risky.

On the one hand, if a stock or ETF moves in the desired direction, margin can help an investor amplify their gains. But if the security in question moves in the opposite direction, it can quickly magnify losses, on top of owing the broker interest on what's borrowed. This dynamic is what makes outstanding margin debt a crude but incredibly useful risk-measuring metric.

Over multiple decades, we'd expect outstanding margin debt to rise in lockstep with the cumulative value of the U.S. stock market. But when margin debt rises in parabolic fashion over a short period, things typically break.

Total Margin Debt hits $1.5 Trillion, a new all-time high 🤯 👀 https://t.co/1IXqZGgrqs

Since 1998, outstanding margin debt has skyrocketed at least 65% over a short timeline on four occasions, the previous three of which were followed by significant stock market declines:

While the AI revolution is fueling risk-taking, we're witnessing possible evidence of a top. Over the previous four months, outstanding margin debt has fallen from $1.502 trillion to $1.448 trillion, as of October.

When investors lighten up their leverage following a parabolic increase, it's historically been the ultimate red flag for Wall Street and investors that a bubble is about to burst.

Though history doesn't always offer the rosiest of short-term outlooks, historical precedent can change drastically depending on investors' perspectives.

In one respect, corrections and bear markets are par for the course when putting your money to work in the stock market. Given that emotions often drive downturns, there isn't much that can be done from a monetary or fiscal policy perspective to stop these double-digit declines from cropping up.

But these downturns share a theme: they're historically short-lived.

Six months ago, the analysts at wealth management firm Bespoke Investment Group calculated the calendar-day length of every S&P 500 bull and bear market since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929. They uncovered a night-and-day difference between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.

The current bull market that began on 10/12/22 is now the 9th longest in S&P 500 history, surpassing the 1,324-day bull that ended on 2/9/1966: https://t.co/4mGsS2t2ft

Whereas the typical S&P 500 bear market has lasted just 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months) over the last 97 years, the average bull market has persisted for approximately 3.6 times as long (1,023 calendar days).

Furthermore, no bear market has taken longer than 630 calendar days to find its trough, according to Bespoke. Meanwhile, just over half (14 of 27) of the S&P 500 bull markets since September 1929 have lasted longer than 630 calendar days.

There isn't a single predictive tool that can tell investors precisely when a stock market downturn will begin, how long it'll last, or how steep the decline will be. But history does conclusively show that these downturns have always represented buying opportunities for optimistic, long-term-minded investors. If the margin debt bubble does burst, opportunity will await.

#3204. Prediction: This Will Be Micron’s Stock Price by the End of 2028

Is Micron's low valuation an attractive entry point?

By Adam Levy – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Micron Technology ›

Few companies have seen their earnings soar amid the artificial intelligence boom like Micron Technology (MU -13.89%). The memory chipmaker has benefited from a spike in demand for its chips, even as it and its competitors take years to ramp up new supply capacity. The result is eye-popping profit margins and a stock price that's gone parabolic.

The stock trades for about $690 per share as of this writing, an impressive 201% gain over the past year and a 598% gain over the past 18 months. Even so, the stock is about 43% off its all-time high reached over the summer.

But as the saying goes, "Past results are not indicative of future returns." Future potential investors need to consider what they can expect from Micron and what that means for the stock price. Here's my prediction for Micron's stock price by the end of 2028.

Micron's earnings growth is directly tied to its ability to charge extremely high prices for memory, specifically high bandwidth memory (HBM), which gets packaged with GPUs and AI accelerators for AI training and inference.

As a result, Micron's gross margin has climbed to an astonishing 87%. But that pricing isn't indicative of a competitive moat, as many high-gross-margin businesses exhibit. Note that rival chipmaker SK Hynix (SKHY -13.11%) produced a gross margin of 86% in its most recent quarter, practically on par with Micron.

The margin strength stems from the supply/demand imbalance. Micron said supply constraints will be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than they were in 2026 in its fourth-quarter earnings presentation. That suggests prices could keep climbing through 2028.

SK Hynix suggested that demand could outpace supply through 2030. But just because demand remains higher than supply doesn't mean prices will keep climbing. Demand has to grow faster than supply.

So, investors expecting prices to continue climbing through 2030 may be mistaken. Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung are set to open and ramp up new production facilities in late 2028.

So, it's likely pricing peaks in 2028 ahead of the massive ramp-up in production capacity. Earnings could peak in late 2028 or early 2029 as a result.

Importantly, as supply constraints ease, prices go down, gross margins decline, and operating costs increase. Once supply reaches equilibrium or exceeds demand, profits can sink quickly. And given the massive amounts memory chipmakers are spending on new capacity, the next downcycle could lead to a big drop in earnings.

The potential for that drop will affect how much investors are willing to pay for the stock's earnings near the cycle peak. A bigger drop-off in earnings will result in a lower multiple on the stock. Micron and its competitors are working to reduce the cyclicality of their businesses by signing long-term agreements with customers, but that may only delay an earnings decline and make the drop-off worse once those contracts expire.

As such, investors are unlikely to pay a very high multiple near Micron's peak earnings. Historically, Micron has commanded a multiple of 3-8 times earnings at its peak. With the potential for a large downcycle, shares are likely to trade in the 3-5-times range, with earnings expected to peak in 2028 or 2029.

It's important to note that the stock price usually peaks before earnings peak. Investors are almost always forward-looking. Any hint that pricing is nearing its peak and earnings are set for a near-term downturn will push the stock lower. We saw that happen last month when Sandisk reported disappointing price improvements for its flash memory NAND chips, and the stock dropped after earnings.

With analysts currently expecting $211 per share in earnings for fiscal 2028 and $218 per share for fiscal 2029, that puts my prediction for Micron's stock price at the end of 2028 somewhere between $610 and $1,040. With the stock trading for $690 right now, it doesn't look like a great time to buy unless you think the earnings cycle will last much longer and the drop-off in earnings will be far less severe once earnings peak.

#3203. iOS 27 lets you use two iPhones with the same phone number

9to5Mac is brought to you by Tello Mobile. Switching to Tello Mobile can bring the cost of your plan down to as little as $5 a month, or an unlimited plan for just $25 a month, all on America’s largest 5G network. See all of the available plans at tello.com.

Among iOS 27’s many new features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces big AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

After iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

#3202. CME vs. Robinhood Markets: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Robinhood's revenue grew far faster than CME's over the latest 12 months, yet its debt load tells a very different story about financial risk.

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 9:20AM EST

10 stocks we like better than CME Group ›

Market volatility often creates opportunities for the platforms that facilitate trading. Deciding between CME Group (CME +0.41%) and Robinhood Markets (HOOD -9.44%) involves weighing the stability of an institutional giant against a fast-growing retail disruptor.

CME Group provides the essential infrastructure for global derivatives trading, offering unmatched liquidity to professional investors. Robinhood Markets has transitioned from a simple trading app to a diversified financial services provider for the modern retail investor. Both companies are positioned to benefit from increased market activity but offer different paths for shareholders.

CME Group operates the world's most diverse derivatives marketplace, offering contracts across interest rates, equities, and commodities in 200 countries. Key partnerships include a 10-year agreement with Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) and a prediction market joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT -1.80%). Because one company accounted for roughly 12% of clearing and transaction fees in its latest report, this customer concentration adds a layer of risk.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $7 billion, an increase of approximately 9% over the prior period. During this time, net income was roughly $4.4 billion as the company benefited from increased trading volumes. CME maintains a high net margin of approximately 63.1%, highlighting its strength among financial stocks.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.1. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the company uses very little borrowed money to fund its operations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly $4.2 billion, reflecting strong cash conversion from its earnings.

Robinhood Markets provides retail brokerage, advisory, and digital banking services to millions of funded customers. Its platform supports trading in traditional assets as well as Bitcoin (BTC +1.81%). It also operates a joint venture with Susquehanna International Group to run an independent futures exchange and clearinghouse.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $5.1 billion, fueled by revenue growth of approximately 21.1%. The company reported net income of close to $2 billion for the same period, reflecting success in scaling its subscription services and interest-earning assets. Its net margin for this time frame was roughly 39%.

As of Robinhood's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 1.3. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $1.6 billion, showing the company's ability to generate cash while expanding.

CME Group faces intense competition from other global exchanges like Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -0.52%) and Nasdaq (NDAQ -0.99%). The company is also subject to regulatory and legislative changes that could impact its clearinghouse and transaction structures. Furthermore, the company manages operational risks related to third-party data centers, highlighted by a cooling failure in November 2025. Cybersecurity threats targeting financial infrastructure also remain a persistent risk for the exchange operator.

Robinhood Markets is sensitive to regulatory scrutiny regarding payment for order flow, which accounts for a substantial portion of its revenue. It competes with established brokerages like Charles Schwab (SCHW -2.13%) and fintech rivals that may have greater capital and brand recognition. The company also depends on a limited number of liquidity providers, such as Virtu Financial (VIRT -4.76%), to execute its trades. Additionally, legal challenges regarding the offering of event contracts could impact Robinhood's future product road map.

Robinhood Markets is cheaper by its P/S ratio, which measures market cap against sales over the past 12 months, while CME Group has a lower forward P/E.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

It's a little hard to pick one over the other because of the current macro environment. Specifically, the market is, as the youths say, crashing out. Robinhood stock is less than a dollar away from its 52-week low. I mean, this year-to-date chart is brutal:

Its stock is also a lot more volatile than CME Group's. Robinhood has seen stronger revenue growth recently, but CME posts a consistently higher profit margin. (This chart's a little wonky because Robinhood didn't go public until 2021.)

In addition to CME's better profitability, I like that it pays a modest dividend yielding about 1.7%.

I think in a somewhat unsettled market like the one we're currently experiencing, a mature, established operator looks like a more attractive stock. Some investors may prefer growth over consistency, in which case, Robinhood may be more appealing. But for me, CME Group gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.
