#3199. ESR Black Friday gift guide: Premium accessories for iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, iPad, AirPods, and Apple Watch

If you picked up a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR says it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

On these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Why it matters: ESR says the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing shows up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Installation is the part most people dread on a brand-new iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and said it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

It’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

The trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

#3198. ASML vs. Broadcom: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

ASML's near-monopoly on chip-printing machines faces off against Broadcom's networking empire, with a sharp valuation gap complicating the choice for growth investors.

By Erin Kennedy – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 9:21AM EST

The semiconductor world is currently split between the machines that build chips and the designs that power them. Is ASML (ASML -6.63%) or Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%) the better play for your portfolio?

ASML holds a virtual monopoly on the advanced lithography machinery required to print the world's most sophisticated microchips. Meanwhile, Broadcom has evolved into a powerhouse of networking components and enterprise software. Both companies are critical to the tech supply chain, but they offer distinct paths for investors seeking exposure to high-end silicon.

ASML manufactures lithography systems, which are massive machines that use light to print intricate patterns onto silicon wafers. It provides the essential hardware for every major chipmaker to produce smaller, faster, and more efficient processors. Because its technology is unique, it serves as a critical gatekeeper for the entire high-end semiconductor market.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $43.4 billion, an increase of roughly 22.5%. The company generated approximately $14.8 billion in net income. This growth highlights the sustained demand for extreme ultraviolet lithography systems used in advanced chip production for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

As of ASML's December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is approximately 1.3. The debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2, showing that the company uses relatively little debt compared to its total equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $12.2 billion.

Broadcom is a dominant player among semiconductor stocks, providing infrastructure software and hardware solutions to global enterprises. The company has significant customer concentration, with its top five end customers accounting for roughly 40% of revenue in its latest annual report. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as evidenced by a $30 billion commitment from Apple (AAPL -1.90%).

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached close to $89.1 billion, representing significant growth of nearly 48.7%. The company reported net income of approximately $38.3 billion during this time frame. This surge was partly driven by the integration of large acquisitions and booming demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure across data centers.

As of Broadcom's November 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 1.7. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.8, indicating a higher level of total debt relative to shareholder equity than ASML. In the fiscal year ended Nov. 2, 2025, free cash flow was close to $26.9 billion, though stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

ASML faces risks from its position at the center of global trade tensions, particularly concerning international export restrictions. The company also operates in the cyclical semiconductor equipment market, where spending by chipmakers can fluctuate based on broader economic conditions and interest rates. Furthermore, the rapid pace of innovation requires constant, heavy investment in research and development to maintain its technological lead over any potential competitors.

Broadcom operates in a highly cyclical industry that faces rapid price erosion and evolving technological requirements driven by artificial intelligence. It relies heavily on a limited number of contract manufacturers, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM -9.48%), which produced approximately 95% of its wafers according to its latest annual report. Broadcom also faces intense regulatory scrutiny and risks associated with its strategy of integrating large acquisitions into its software portfolio.

Broadcom looks potentially cheaper based on its forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, whereas ASML has a lower P/S ratio.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The current market environment is, shall we say, hostile to tech stocks, and shares of ASML and Broadcom reflect that:

That said, zooming out over the past decade, both stocks have put in decent performances, handily outpacing the S&P 500's (^GSPC -3.70%) return:

In the past, I have picked ASML over many other stocks for several reasons. For one, it has a monopoly in the extreme ultraviolet lithography niche it operates in. That gives it strong pricing power and a solid moat. ASML also consistently reports a net margin in excess of 30%, and it pays a modest dividend.

However, it's hard to argue with Broadcom's long-term performance. A company of that size reporting nearly 50% revenue growth is pretty wild. ASML and Broadcom are both exposed to the inherent cyclicality of the semiconductor industry, so I think that risk factor offsets itself. And the tech sector (and the market in general) may be melting down right now, but long-term investors shouldn't get especially concerned over what happens in the course of a week, or a month, or even a year.

I'm breaking with my pattern here. I don't think ASML is a bad choice, to be clear, but Broadcom has strong margins and even better revenue growth. Broadcom gets my vote for 2027 and beyond.

#3195. Not Anthropic. Not SpaceX. This Is the AI Stock to Buy for the Long Term

Under-the-radar chip stock On Semiconductor trades at a compelling value, and the company has impressive long-term growth prospects.

By Lee Samaha – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:22AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

The Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) initial public offering (IPO) this week reinforced the view that, despite recent turbulence related to developments at Nvidia, investment in artificial intelligence (AI) remains in high-growth mode. That's not in doubt; still, the key question for retail investors is how to find the best-value way to invest in it. Companies like the AI lab and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%), with its AI infrastructure, rocket launch, and connectivity businesses, appear attractive on this basis. Still, I think there's another company that's a better buy on a risk-adjusted basis: On Semiconductor (ON -7.42%).

To buy into the investment theme, you need to believe that the use of AI applications will continue to grow, spurring growth for AI enterprises like Anthropic and, in turn, demand for SpaceX's data center infrastructure. While these assumptions about the outlook for end demand seem entirely feasible, the reality is that both companies are engaged in a fiercely competitive, highly capital-intensive arms race.

In Anthropic's case, it needs to continually and heavily invest in leasing compute capacity from infrastructure services (including those from SpaceX) to compete for frontier model supremacy with its rivals -- a group that actually includes SpaceX. Anthropic has already made over $900 billion in spending commitments, including $120.5 billion in an agreement with SpaceX.

In turn, compute providers like SpaceX and the well-known hyperscalers are having to make massive investments into new data center capacity to meet their contractual obligations. These investments are not risk-free. In SpaceX's case in particular, there are serious questions about how quickly its planned orbital data center satellites will depreciate. SpaceX also faces launch risk every time it attempts to send any cargo into space, and if it merges with Tesla, the company will be part of a much larger and more complex business.

All told, if there's any slowdown in demand for AI applications, both Anthropic and SpaceX are likely to suffer disproportionately.

The power and sensing chip company is largely a play on the increasing power density, not only in its core automotive and industrial end markets, but also in its fast-growing data center business. The company is best known for power control chips and sensing technology that are used in electric vehicles (EVs), as well as myriad industrial applications ranging from EV charging and industrial automation to renewable energy and consumer electronics.

As an investment, On Semiconductor is not without risk. Its core automotive business is exposed to the cyclicality of the EV market; the power semiconductor market is competitive, and there's execution risk around its recent AI-related acquisitions. However, the diversity of its end markets means it doesn't face the same degree of existential risk as companies like Anthropic and SpaceX do from frontier model competition and capital-intensive investments.

In contrast to many AI-related companies, On Semiconductor is highly cash-generative, with Wall Street analysts targeting $2 billion in free cash flow (FCF) for 2027 and $2.3 billion for 2028, according to Visible Alpha. Based on its current market cap of $25.1 billion, the stock would be trading at 12.6 times FCF in 2027 and 10.9 times FCF in 2028.

Those are highly attractive valuations for any company whose management is targeting 30% annual operating income growth from 2026 to 2030. In that period, its data center revenue growth is expected to grow at a 50% annual rate.

On top of all of this, On Semiconductor's power and sensing solutions are set to become a key feature of physical AI solutions (such as robots, EVs, drones, and industrial machines) over the long term. As more physical AI products are developed, there will be an increasing need for edge power density. For example, robots can't wait a few seconds for calculations in the cloud; they need to process sensory inputs in real time, which requires power and sensing chips.

As such, the company has significant exposure to a major AI investment theme, but doesn't trade at a nosebleed valuation, and doesn’t carry the kind of downside risk inherent in other pure-play AI stocks.

#3193. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3189. Proton Pass is up to 60% off for Black Friday, and it does way more than just store your passwords

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Proton Pass is designed to take that friction out of your day. It creates strong, unique passwords, remembers them for you, and fills them in when you log in. But it also handles something a password alone can’t: keeping your real email address out of another retailer’s database.

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other important parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

Proton Pass does that work for you. When you sign up for a website, its password generator can create a strong password that’s completely unique. Save it in your vault, and Proton Pass can fill in your credentials when you return.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

#3188. Here's How Much $2,500 in General Mills Stock Could Pay You in Dividends in 2027

Is General Mills' frozen dividend a red flag or a smart turnaround move? See what a $2,500 investment pays in 2027 while this consumer staples leader works through a tough economy.

By Anders Bylund – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:37AM EST

10 stocks we like better than General Mills ›

General Mills (GIS +3.65%) is in the middle of a multi-year turnaround. Early operating metrics suggest the effort is gaining traction in 2026.

After years of post-pandemic price hikes pushed budget-conscious shoppers toward store brands, the Minneapolis-based food giant rolled back everyday prices across two-thirds of its North American retail portfolio. The strategy has helped narrow market-share losses in key categories. Core brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch, and Lucky Charms are back to growing, while new high-protein snacks and fresh pet foods are catching on.

Of course, General Mills also broke a long-standing habit by leaving its quarterly dividend parked at $0.61 per share rather than bumping it up this past summer. Honestly, I hope the board keeps it frozen for another couple of years. When you are trying to revitalize legacy brands, absorb rising wheat and freight costs, and trim debt, hanging on to extra cash for active turnaround plays is just smart business 101.

It's OK if that brand boost and distribution revamp takes a while, as long as General Mills gets it done.

Still, history offers a useful lantern for long-term shareholders navigating an inflationary squeeze. Demand for name-brand consumer staples tends to meander during periods of acute economic stress, as households trade down to store brands and discount alternatives. In the 1970s, double-digit inflation severely tested consumer purchasing power before cooling to roughly 4% in the 1980s and lower still in subsequent decades.

Across those cycles, investors who accumulated shares of durable, brand-leading businesses with reliable dividend policies were consistently rewarded once household budgets stabilized. General Mills fits that profile, flaunting category leaders like Cheerios, Nature Valley, Pillsbury, and Blue Buffalo. These household brands are not going away.

"Lucky Charms is back to growth, and Reese's Puffs is back to growth, and Cinnamon Toast Crunch is back to growth," CEO Jeff Harmening said on the Q1 2027 earnings call in September. "And that has nothing to do with anything to do with pricing. It has to do with really good marketing and really good product news."

So what does that patience actually pay while you wait for the recovery? Let's run the numbers using General Mills' Nov. 19 closing price of $34.48 per share. Putting approximately $2,500 to work at that price gets you roughly 73 shares of stock.

Assuming the board holds the quarterly dividend steady at $0.61 per share throughout next year, as it did over the last year and a half, those 73 shares would generate $178.12 in dividend income during 2027 (or roughly $178). At today's prices, that's an annualized yield of nearly 7.1%.

Better yet, you aren't paying a steep price for that cash flow. At roughly 10.1 times forward earnings and 11.9 times trailing free cash flow, the stock is priced like Cheerios are going out of style. Call me biased, but my breakfast bowl disagrees.

If you believe in the staying power of these household brands, locking in a roughly 7% yield at a bargain valuation sets you up nicely for brisk total returns once the consumer storm finally passes. After rain comes sunshine, and General Mills will pay dividends in both weather patterns.

#3186. The Nasdaq Just Triggered a Correction. 1 Move I'm Making Right Now -- and 1 I'm Avoiding

Now is a good time to keep buying stocks if you’re diversified and focused on the long term.

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF ›

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC -3.70%) includes the 500 largest publicly traded companies in America. Its name is often interchangeable with "the stock market" because the 500 large-cap stocks in this index make up about 80% of the total U.S. stock market capitalization.

So, when "the stock market" (as in the S&P 500) loses more than 10% of its value in a month, people get nervous. As of Nov. 20, since reaching its record high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 is down about 11.6%.

The biggest driver of this recent stock market swoon is the same reason stocks have been delivering such strong results since 2022: the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Big-spending AI hyperscalers and innovative AI frontier labs have been buoyed by investor enthusiasm for futuristic technology that promises to boost productivity and economic growth.

But to get to that bright future, these AI companies have been spending (and borrowing) hundreds of billions of dollars. Investors are starting to balk at the high price of AI. As a result of these AI fears, the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has fallen even further than the S&P 500. The tech sector benchmark is down about 20% since Oct. 6 -- heading into a bear market.

It's understandable to feel nervous when the stock market is falling like this, but investors need to take heart, stay calm, and have confidence in the future. If you've been investing as long as I have (or longer), you've lived through worse than this.

Here's one move I'm making with my investments right now and one I'm avoiding.

It's easy to say and harder to do, but it's true: When stock prices are plummeting, that's when I try to just keep buying more stocks. A 10% stock market correction or a 20% (or worse) bear market is ironically the best time to buy stocks. It means stocks are "on sale."

So that's what I'm doing. I'm going to keep buying stocks in a diversified portfolio of low-cost index funds. My favorite U.S. index fund is the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI -3.52%) because it lets me own 3,511 U.S. stocks of all sizes and industries, not just the tech sector.

Additionally, times when the U.S. stock market is struggling can be good occasions to diversify with international stocks. I'm going to keep buying the Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (VXUS -3.27%) and its remarkably diversified portfolio of 8,874 stocks from dozens of other countries beyond the U.S. market.

Eviedence shows that corrections and bear markets are temporary. If you look at the long run of stock market history, the S&P 500 has always bounced back from even the biggest stock market crashes and economic crises.

Because I'm diversified with a portfolio of thousands of stocks from the U.S. and around the world, I believe that there's never a "bad time" to buy stocks. The stock market might keep falling for a while, even after I buy my next shares -- that's OK. I don't know which individual companies or industries will be the winners or losers -- that's fine, too. By owning these index funds, I'm betting on the stock market itself to sort out the winners for me.

Buying "all the stocks" this way lets me own a piece of the global economy’s long-term upside.

It's usually a bad idea for investors to sell stocks during a bear market. It's a little like selling a car or a house that's underwater on the loan -- it puts you in a disadvantaged position and locks in your losses.

(The only exception is if you have individual stock positions that you no longer believe in and want to sell at a loss for tax-loss harvesting purposes. That's a longer conversation to be had with a professional tax advisor.)

With a diversified portfolio of index funds that I'm holding for the long term, I'm not looking to sell anything right now. That's because I don't need the money out of my investment portfolio right now; I need it 20 or 30 years in the future. I don't need to liquidate my investment portfolio for cash. I don't need my stocks to go up today or tomorrow or next year. I need them to deliver long-term returns for the next 20 years or more.

#3185. Meta Is Trying to Woo Teens to Instagram Through Schools

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Project Gryffindor is an initiative intended to make Instagram popular by marketing "school communities" on the platform.

Meta has justifiably attracted more scrutiny than ever this year, along with multibillion-dollar judgments and settlements, over how its business practices affect young social media users. The company, however, is not retreating.

In fact, the tech giant has made a major push toward drawing teenagers to one of its flagship platforms, Instagram, by targeting them at their schools.

According to documents obtained and reported by NPR, Meta launched an initiative called Project Gryffindor, named after a Hogwarts house in the Harry Potter series, to create school communities on Instagram in order to boost user counts and engagement on the platform.

Meta’s goal of approaching young users where they spend the most time offline was not a secret. As recently as late September, the company said it was expanding its School Partnership Program, which includes 17,000 schools, with a stated goal to “help students and parents stay informed.”

The company’s internal documents reveal some of the motivations behind Meta’s push for school adoption and Project Gryffindor’s proposed features, such as school banners on teen profiles and the ability to search school directories by class year. The details were acquired as part of discovery in a multistate lawsuit over whether social media platforms are designed to be addictive to users under 18. Meta is a defendant in the case, along with other companies, including TikTok, Snap and Google.

In 2024, Instagram introduced Teen accounts and has since been trying to assure parents they’re safe while rolling out additional protections. Studies, however, have suggested that young teens regularly encounter unsafe content or deal with unwanted contact. Recruiting more users at an early age without resolving these risks could make teens more vulnerable to mental health issues and increase the chances of being bullied or harassed.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Like other social platforms, Instagram primarily makes its money from targeted advertising. User retention is a key part of Meta’s strategy.

In one of the document slides, titled “Why schools, why now?” which preceded Gryffindor’s launch, Meta said, “Competitors are exploring school social use cases, but IG may be better positioned for school connections thanks to our differentiator of meeting new people and building relationships with acquaintances.” In other words, Instagram’s size and scale, with about 3 billion active users globally, automatically make it a draw for students.

The NPR report comes within a week of a filing against Meta alleging that it’s withholding evidence in a major case involving social media’s effects on teenagers.

One of Meta’s marketing pitches for its School Partnership Program is that it’s trying to create online safe spaces for students, while giving parents and schools more oversight on what’s accessible on the platform. But experts warn that Meta’s history makes it hard to trust the company with protecting kids from predators or scammers.

Katie Paul, director of the Center for Accountability’s Tech Transparency Project, which has been researching how Meta handles child-safety issues, said that Instagram Teen accounts “are not safe as advertised” and that nothing is “legally requiring the company to make these safe.” Paul pointed out that Instagram launched these accounts only when lawsuits over social media harm started rolling in.

“It’s all part of a broader marketing (effort) to claim that these are just safer for kids because they are Teen accounts,” Paul said. That marketing effort has included paid endorsements from therapists, psychologists and parent influencers to promote Teen accounts. The case for building up partnerships with schools is a way of “passing the buck on responsibility” to schools and parents, Paul said.

Parents, in particular, have less power in Instagram’s school groups: Unlike the school administrators tasked with managing school groups, parents have no powers to moderate or manage those groups; they can only view them. For Teen accounts in general, parents can’t view direct messages sent to or received by their children.

Meta’s business interests in its push for student engagement and school partnerships are easy to see through. Because kids are likely to be lifetime users on these platforms, getting them hooked early has long-term financial value.

“Ultimately, Meta is the one profiting off of the data collection of these kids while simultaneously failing to keep them safe,” Paul said.

#3184. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security leaders reveal the future consequences of AI outpacing human defenders.

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

#3182. The Stock Market Just Had Its Worst Week of 2026. Here's Why Long-Term Investors Shouldn't Flinch.

Investors should be prepared for this ahead of time.

By David Dierking – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:45AM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

The U.S. midterm election has ushered in some of the most stock market volatility we've seen since the start of the Iran war. In the two days following Election Day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.93%) experienced both its best and worst trading sessions since April 2025. The 2.7% decline for the week as a whole is also the worst in 19 months.

Since we haven't seen a week like this in a while, you might think it's rare. It isn't. If you're a long-term investor and reacted to virtually any of the trading days we've seen this month, it might be worth reconsidering just how small the move was in the bigger picture.

The election-week losses have helped push the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) to nearly 7% below its all-time high. But those kinds of pullbacks have actually been fairly normal over even just the past year.

That's three separate incidents over just the past year before what happened in November. Their relatively quick turnarounds may have made them largely forgettable. But pullbacks like this are far more common than you might think.

But it's the speed of the recoveries that has made these pullbacks especially dangerous. If you saw the S&P 500 falling and decided to sell in order to protect yourself, you had almost no time to buy back in before it was too late.

And that's the biggest problem with trying to time the market. The typical outcome is you lock in the losses after selling, but you miss out on the subsequent rebound. All you've essentially done is damage your portfolio's returns.

That's why long-term investors shouldn't flinch. These kinds of 5%-10% declines in the S&P 500 are normal and should be expected when investing in equities. It's simply the price of admission to the stock market.

Trying to react to short-term volatility is usually a bad idea. If you're a long-term investor, riding out the ups and downs is the key to success.

#3180. Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple is leaning into AI-powered health tools with the launch of its Apple Health AI Usage Study.

Apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google launched its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

If you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.

#3178. GTA 6 Launch Day Hits Different for Fired Rockstar Workers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Three people among the bigger group fired from Rockstar last year describe the "bittersweetness" of finally seeing the game they poured their hearts into out in the world.

As people across the world sneak a day away from the office to play the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, the Rockstar employees who made the game are hopefully enjoying a well-earned day off in celebration. But not everyone who worked on the cultural juggernaut is joining the victory lap.

For the 34 workers based in the UK and Canada who Rockstar dismissed in October 2025, GTA 6 launch day isn’t the day of celebration it should’ve been.

“I should be with my team, taking a photo at every poster I can see, and be happy about it,” says Branimira Yordanova, who worked for three years in the lighting department at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, Scotland. “But it’s impossible because of how much hurt the firing has caused everyone.”

Rockstar fired the workers on the spot — something that’s only legal in the UK in cases of gross misconduct — alleging that they’d shared confidential company information on a Discord server.

The workers tell a different story. They say the company had long been aware of the Discord server, and only fired them when it started to look as though their efforts to unionize might succeed. They believe they were made an example of.

On the evening before the game’s launch, I spoke with Yordanova and her former colleague Dayne Oram, a senior production coordinator who had been at Rockstar for seven years and was also affected by the dismissals, about how they were feeling about launch day.

“One of our fellow colleagues said it the best,” says Yordanova. “What we’ll feel tomorrow is mourning what could have been, whether we want to or not.”

For all those who are mourning, others among the fired workers still hold a candle for GTA. Jacob Jones, who spent one year as a game tester before taking a role as a designer on the open world team for four years, was raring to play the game on launch day.

Jones graduated from being a childhood fan of the franchise – even counting the signatures of Rockstar co-founders Sam and Dan Hauser among his merch collection – to his dream job. He remains a GTA fan to this day, but describes feeling a sense of “poignance” and “bittersweetness” toward the launch.

For Oram, Yordanova and Jones, GTA 6 eve was already a heavy day, even aside from the launch fever.

They’re all part of a case brought by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain on behalf of 23 former Rockstar North employees, who say they were unfairly dismissed for union activity. Hours before Oram and Yordanova spoke with me, a Glasgow employment tribunal had heard Rockstar’s closing submissions, which now leaves the fired workers in limbo as they wait for a verdict.

Rockstar North maintains that it fired the employees for gross misconduct. The company didn’t respond to a request for further comment.

Oram, Yordanova and Jones all speak highly of their former colleagues and teams, but Oram calls the sacking a “traumatic experience.” Only Yordanova managed to secure alternative employment in the past 13 months. Jones says for now he’s focused on getting justice.

Meanwhile, reminders of their former employer have been everywhere as the studio geared up to release perhaps the most highly anticipated game of all time. Billboards, buses and online ads have been impossible to avoid, leaving Yordanova feeling “devastated.”

“I’ve genuinely had to make sure to avoid looking at it,” she says. “It’s such a cool game, and to know that you worked on it, you feel a sense of pride and joy to see it out. But it’s like that sense of joy has been taken away from us in such a ruthless manner.”

Oram acknowledges having “mixed feelings” about the launch. It’s been fantastic watching video footage of people playing and reviewing the game, they say. At the same time, they’ve found it difficult not being able to celebrate the moment with their former team.

The workers fired from Rockstar North had varying ideas about whether they wanted to celebrate the launch, or avoid it entirely. Jones is one of those who started playing the game as soon as he got home from the tribunal at 1 a.m. By the time we spoke on Thursday, he’d played around six or seven hours.

“I personally think it’s a masterpiece,” he says. Even though he worked on the game, he’s discovering surprises everywhere. “I haven’t completed it yet, but I do think it is probably the greatest game ever made.”

Oram says that they planned to stick with watching streams of the game on launch day. “I’m probably not going to play the game for a little while, but I am looking forward to at least watching some people,” they say. Oram worked across so many bits of the game that there’s plenty they’re excited to see people discover.

Yordanova says she’s firmly in the avoidance camp. “I was really excited about playing the game in its official form because obviously when you work on it, you get to play it,” she says. “Even while we were in the office, there were parts I was really excited about – but I don’t think I’ll be playing it for the foreseeable future.”

She hopes that one day her feelings will change, she adds. “But right now, that’s just not possible in any way.”

Instead, she’ll be spending the day with friends who supported her over the last year. She plans to “dive into another art form” by seeing the stop-motion animated film Wildwood at the cinema, which particularly appeals to her as a lighting artist.

Many people playing GTA 6 around the world won’t be aware of what happened to Oram, Yordanova, Jones and their colleagues during the game’s development, but the affected workers would like people to know. “I understand people just want to focus on the joy, but I don’t think you can separate the launch with what happened,” says Yordanova.

Reflecting on what happened, Jones says it’s such a shame the way things went down. “It was my absolute passion,” he says. “I just wish that the circumstances were different, and I would have loved to have still been there working on games. I wish I got to the end.”

Correction, Nov. 20: An earlier version of this article stated that none of the three fired Rockstar workers had secured further work, which is not the case.

#3177. Oura’s new feature could help you kick jet lag – how to enable it

Oura just launched a Jet Lag Plan to help you stay alert when you switch time zones, whether you're traveling for business or pleasure.

Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.

Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura announced Jet Lag Plan, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.

Also: Oura Ring users may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know

Jet Lag Plan takes into account your travel itinerary, sleep patterns, and body responses to provide guidance for traveling members entering new time zones.

Jet lag happens when circadian rhythms are at odds with local time zones, but there are a few things people can do to adjust.

Oura factors in the direction of travel, how many time zones are crossed, individual light windows, and sleep timing.

Ring users will enter their flight details, including information like multi-stop trips, and also include the reason for the trip. Oura adjusts the Jet Lag Plan accordingly, and a business trip’s plan may differ in intensity from that of a vacation.

“Two people on the same flight can get different plans, because guidance reflects your itinerary, your typical sleep schedule, and your chronotype,” Oura writes in a blog post. The chronotype refers to Oura’s sleep chronotype, which categorizes users into six types (early morning, morning, early evening, and so on) based on their historical sleep activity.

After adding these details, Oura provides each user with timely guidance throughout their trip. This guidance could include recommendations on when to begin or end caffeine consumption or light exposure, and when to start preparing for sleep. The plan is designed for those crossing three or more time zones. Members can follow along with these recommendations by checking them off as they complete each one. #3176. Own 2 Android phones? Google may let you switch service fast – like iPhone Handoff

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If Android Fast Switch works like iPhone Handoff, one eSIM can be quickly switched between two phones.

In iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows users to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones. Text strings in Google’s SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a similar feature for compatible Android phones, according to Android Authority.

Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch. Little information is currently available about the feature’s limitations, including which phones or mobile carriers may not be compatible.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart

On Apple’s side, any iPhone in the US running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM can use iPhone Handoff. AT&T does not currently support iPhone Handoff.

However, the code strings uncovered by Android Authority show that Android’s Fast Switch will work similarly to iPhone Handoff, in that users must be signed in to both devices under the same Google account for the feature to work.

Strings in Google’s SIM Manager app also point to no sharing between two users, so this feature isn’t a way to circumvent carrier fees by adding service to someone else’s phone for the price of one.

If Fast Switch works anything like iPhone Handoff, which it appears it will, one eSIM can be switched between two phones. So, calls, messages, location services, and other information synced to your Apple ID can remain consistent between two devices.

Also: 5 hidden iOS 27 features that make older iPhones better

Some third-party apps, like banking, communications, or social media, may also remain consistent across the two phones, depending on the app’s syncing behavior.

Features like Apple’s iPhone Handoff and Google’s Fast Switch are ideal for people who regularly use two phones. Business owners and digital creators may want one phone strictly for business purposes and the other for personal use.

Also: Google Wallet turns your Android phone into a digital house key

In that case, one person can keep up with two phones without paying for two phone service lines through their carrier. Still, users will incur a fee, as T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month.
