Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates rose enough today that you might be feeling some sticker shock.

If you're here looking for lower mortgage interest rates, today is definitely not your day.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage jumped to 7.38% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points higher than yesterday and 12 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Keep in mind that mortgage rates are always on the move, and that if you're tracking rates day-to-day, you're going to see a lot of volatility. Zooming out and looking at the bigger picture — like a graph showing at least a month's worth of rate data — can help you see the overall trend.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.88% or higher — but there aren’t many people for whom that’s true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3099. 1 Growth ETF I'm Buying Even When the Market Is Expensive

There'll be short-term volatility, but the long-term appeal is still strong.

By Stefon Walters – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF ›

Many tech or tech-adjacent companies have seen their valuations surge during the current AI boom. Of course, this has been good for investors who were along for the ride, but one "downside" is how expensive the market has become.

Depending on the metric you're using, the last time the market was this expensive was during the dot-com bubble, which didn't necessarily end with investors throwing confetti. That said, even with the market this expensive, it's not a bad time to pick up a quality growth ETF, especially with notable ones falling over the past month.

One worth considering is the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM -5.42%), which has thrived over the years but is down over 8% in the past month.

QQQM mirrors the Nasdaq-100, an index that tracks the 100 largest non-financial stocks trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange. Although it doesn't have "growth" in its name like other popular growth-focused ETFs, it's just as qualified to be considered one.

This ETF has only been trading since October 2020, but the Nasdaq-100 has been around for 41 years and has routinely outperformed the S&P 500.

Source: YCharts. Averages based on closing levels on Nov. 17.

Over the past 20 years, the Nasdaq-100 has outperformed the S&P 500 15 times. Its bad slumps have been worse than the S&P 500's, but that's what you expect from a growth stock or ETF. Past results don't guarantee future performance, but I see this trend continuing, as the tech sector has a bit more runway ahead.

Right now, QQQM has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- which tells you how much you're paying per $1 of a company's earnings -- of 27.02, which is historically expensive. That could make the fund more volatile in the short term or limit immediate upside, but it doesn't take away from its long-term appeal.

The current AI arms race will strongly influence QQQM's performance, but even beyond that, it holds companies across other sectors that act as a crutch and present different non-tech growth opportunities.

One thing to keep an eye on is the overlap between QQQM and popular investments like an S&P 500 ETF. QQQM and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%), for example, share seven of the same top 10 holdings:

Sources: Invesco and Vanguard. QQQM percentages as of Nov. 16; VOO percentages as of Oct. 31.

Growth ETFs, whether QQQM or another, can be great portfolio pieces, but they can be redundant if you're investing in the same companies across multiple funds. Over 80% of QQQM's holdings are also in the S&P 500. That doesn't mean you can't invest in both; just be intentional about how much exposure you want to a handful of stocks.

I wouldn't make QQQM the bulk of my portfolio (despite its historical outperformance) because of its heavy tech concentration, but it could be a great supplemental piece.

#3098. 3 High-Yield Dividend Stocks to Buy Now and 2 to Avoid Despite the Yield

Among high-yield dividend stocks, there are some diamonds in the rough, but beware of the "yield traps" as well.

By Thomas Niel – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:31AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vici Properties ›

High-yield dividend stocks often result from a falling share price. In many cases, this is a red flag. When investors bail on a dividend stock, it's typically due to falling confidence in future results. Deteriorating financial performance can, in turn, lead to dividend cuts or, worse, suspensions.

That said, there are a few diamonds in the rough, like Enterprise Products Partners (EPD -0.91%), VICI Properties (VICI +0.04%)and Verizon Communications (VZ +1.62%). Conversely, there are dividend stocks with such severe "yield trap" status that they are instant candidates for the "avoid" pile, like Fidelity National Information Services (FIS -0.42%) and Icahn Enterprises (IEP -7.31%).

Enterprise Products Partners is a master limited partnership (MLP) that owns and operates midstream energy assets, such as oil and gas pipelines. Units in this MLP have a forward dividend yield of around 6.15%. Enterprise Products Partners also has a nearly 30-year track record of consecutive dividend growth.

Over the last decade, the MLP's quarterly payouts, known as distributions, have increased by an average of 3.6% annually. This trend appears sustainable, given the percentage of cash flow devoted not only to distributions but also to stock buybacks. Per the MLP's latest quarterly earnings release, it used just 54% of its cash flow from operations (CFFO) for return-of-capital purposes, with the remainder reinvested in the business. For comparison, most major MLPs and pipeline-owning C-corps have payout ratios of 60% and above.

Speaking of growth, management has guided for $2.9 billion to $3.4 billion in growth-related capital spending. While not providing concrete guidance for future growth, Enterprise Products Partners has grown discretionary cash flow (DCF) from around $0.90 to $4.07 per share, or around 7.9% annualized. I wouldn't necessarily expect Enterprise to keep growing at such a clip, but even at a lesser extent, steady cash flow growth could lead to solid long-term total returns.

VICI Properties is a real estate investment trust (REIT) specializing in casino real estate; it has since expanded to own such properties from other major gaming companies, including MGM Resorts and Golden Entertainment.

This gives REIT ownership of much of the Las Vegas Strip, as well as real estate holdings across numerous regional casino markets in the United States and overseas. VICI Properties currently has a forward dividend yield of around 7.5%. The REIT has increased its distributions for six consecutive years, with payout growth over the last five years averaging nearly 10%. Having said this, the increase in distributions has diminished more recently. The latest dividend increase, for instance, came in at just 2.2%.

Talk of rising interest rates has put pressure on VICI Properties, as it has on REIT stocks across the board. The pending leveraged buyout of Caesars by Fertitta Entertainment also creates some uncertainty over future rental income. Nevertheless, as the REIT continues to report solid results, including an increase in adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) per share, the REIT's equivalent of earnings per share (EPS), it remains a strong long-term choice for capital growth and a high dividend yield.

Verizon Communications is a legacy telco, built primarily from the regional Bell operating companies spun off from the old AT&T in the 1980s. Verizon's background may be what gives it its blue chip dividend stock status, but in more recent years, its legacy has been more of a liability than an asset.

Fidelity National Information Services is a leading banking and payment technology company. With a 6.6% forward dividend yield and its low valuation of just 5 times forward earnings, this fintech may at first seem like a bargain buy, but take a closer look at the reasons behind its high yield and low valuation.

So far this year, shares have fallen by over 60%, with the stock tumbling 24% alone following its Q3 2026 earnings release earlier this month. Chalk this up to continued guidance downgrades, largely due to banks delaying their move to the company's subscription-based software products. The company also has a large debt load from past acquisitions and has decided to pause buybacks to focus on deleveraging.

The company's latest efforts have yet to lead to a dividend cut, and its payout ratio remains relatively low at around 25.7%. However, with earnings expected to drop next year and Fidelity National's history of dividend cuts, this isn't off the table. Worse yet, even if the dividend stays as is, a further deterioration in operating performance could cause the resulting stock price drop to outweigh the benefit of the company's higher-than-average yield. Until results and guidance appear more promising, consider this a "stay away" situation among dividend stocks.

Icahn Enterprises is an MLP controlled by billionaire financier Carl Icahn. However, it is not like your typical MLP that owns pipelines or other natural resource assets. Instead, it operates like a holding company, with its main assets including a majority stake in refiner CVR Energy. Icahn also has holdings in other operating companies, real estate, and $1.4 billion invested in funds managed by the famed investor.

Icahn Enterprises has long had one of the highest forward dividend yields among U.S.-listed stocks. However, its nearly 71% forward yield is very misleading. For one, Carl Icahn, who owns 87.7% of the outstanding units, receives his quarterly distributions in newly issued units, not cash. The MLP has also relied on the sale of new units to fund cash dividends. In other words, outside investors are trading a high yield for high shareholder dilution.

This dynamic, coupled with its recurring high investment losses and recent credit downgrade, helps to explain why this stock has lost nearly 95% of its value over the last five years. Although shares may be reaching the point where they trade below breakup value, with debt and investment loss concerns and concerns about a dividend cut persisting, a further drop appears likely.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

#3095. Asked on Reddit: I Lost My Job; What Should I Do First?

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income loss is stressful; the first steps involve cutting costs and focusing on essentials.

A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.

Should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty? Or is it better to rely on the severance payout to handle expenses?

Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.

For more ideas, I asked three financial experts how to manage money in the immediate aftermath of job loss.

While it’s tempting to make quick decisions about tapping into a retirement fund or selling a house, it’s better to wait on any big moves, says Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor at the financial firm Daniel A. White & Associates in Lewes, Delaware.

That’s because you need time to digest the situation and weigh the pros and cons of different options, he says. “People can get impulsive and panic, and it’s usually a bad thing to make decisions when you’re panicking,” he says.

Take your time, get second opinions and think through all of your options first, Wine suggests.

If you’re fortunate enough to receive a severance package, wait to sign it until you’ve reviewed it carefully and understand all of the details, says John Rafferty, partner and investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana.

For example, make sure you know about your health insurance options, such as whether you’ll receive insurance through COBRA or need to take out a new policy in the health insurance marketplace.

Filing for unemployment and checking into any other available workplace benefits — such as help with your new job search — is also an important part of understanding what support to expect in the weeks and months ahead, Rafferty adds.

Creating a bare-bones budget stripped of “extras” like restaurant meals or travel can help the severance payment last as long as possible, Rafferty says.

“Now that you don’t have income coming in, ask yourself, ‘How much can I spend and where?’”

You might be able to cut back on entertainment costs, coffee runs and clothing purchases, for example.

At the same time, it’s important to prioritize the essentials like mortgage payments, rent, utilities and food. Rafferty recommends calling your mortgage company, utilities provider and any other lenders to ask if they have a hardship program for those experiencing financial challenges.

Opting in could give you more time to pay your bills or temporarily lower payments.

It’s hard to stick to a budget that eliminates all entertainment, so Rafferty suggests finding enjoyable activities that come with a low price tag. Hiking, discovering a new park and participating in free community events are all ways to enjoy downtime on a budget.

“Having that release is mentally a big thing so you can stay prepared for the job search,” he says. “Otherwise, it’s easy to get down and feel negative, and we need things to help us feel positive.”

Similarly, connecting with friends and family during this time is crucial, says Laura Adams, accredited financial counselor and financial coach in Wilmington, North Carolina.

People often feel a sense of shame or embarrassment after job loss, and Adams encourages people to talk about their feelings and ask for help if needed. “Financial shame can cause us to make emotional rather than confident financial decisions,” she says.

Starting some kind of side hustle to bring in extra cash can also help bridge the gap between the job loss and your next job, Wine says. Substitute teaching, working at a local public golf course and driving for a rideshare service are all options he’s seen people try.

Doing something new also helps stave off boredom while unemployed, but he cautions that you’ll still owe taxes on any side income you bring in, so plan accordingly.

All three financial experts also emphasized that a job loss is easier to handle with an emergency savings fund you can turn to, and suggested building one up — ideally three to six months’ worth of expenses. But starting small helps, too — while employed, if possible.

The Redditor who posted the question mentioned that, like many Americans, they lacked emergency savings. This added urgency to the question of what to prioritize.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like how to deal with job loss, so we sifted through Reddit forums to get a pulse check. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

#3093. Billionaire Investor Philippe Laffont Just Highlighted 2 Companies He Expects to Be Big Winners of the Agentic AI Era

The rise of agentic AI could boost plenty of businesses, but Laffont is putting his money into Intel and Meta Platforms.

By Adam Levy – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:44AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Meta Platforms ›

Philippe Laffont built his hedge fund, Coatue Management, on his ability to identify major technology trends and the companies that stand to benefit most from them ahead of the crowd. In his latest update for investors about the outlook for the public market, he laid out a bull case for agentic AI.

It's easy to assert that the ability for AI agents to complete tasks for anyone could be a major transformational technology, but figuring out which companies are best positioned to profit from that transformation is a much tougher task. Laffont doesn't leave investors hanging, though. He identified two that he views as likely winners from the agentic AI era: Meta Platforms (META -5.93%) and Intel (INTC -7.97%).

Here's the case for both and whether the stocks are worth buying right now.

Meta launched its Muse consumer AI agent in September, and the app saw near-instant success. It counted 10 million users within a month and a half of its release, according to CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Laffont and his team at Coatue describe the shift from Meta's feed-based apps to Muse as a shift from monetizing attention to monetizing intent. While Meta has managed to collect huge amounts of data on its users that make it unparalleled at monetizing attention, explicit intent is much easier to monetize — just ask Google or Amazon.

Meta's plan is to take a small cut from every transaction that Muse processes on behalf of its users. Laffont estimates that in 2031, agentic AI commerce could account for $2.5 trillion in global gross merchandise volume. At a 10% take rate for AI agents, that's $250 billion in potential revenue, more than Meta's total revenue over the last 12 months.

Meta's advertising business continues to grow as well, as advances in AI make its feeds more engaging and its ads more relevant to the people they are displayed to. That's evidenced by the increase in both price per ad and total ad impressions in each of the last 12 quarters. Coatue's analysts believe annual ad revenue per daily active user will climb from $68 this year to $153 by 2031.

With Meta's stock trading for about 21.5 times forward earnings estimates, it looks like a bargain if it delivers that expected revenue and earnings growth. In the third quarter, Laffont increased Coatue's Meta position by 79% from the prior quarter, boosting it to 6% of the hedge fund’s public equity portfolio. The early successes of Muse could push him to buy more.

Training AI requires enormous amounts of data to be handled by arrays of parallel processors — the most common of which are GPUs — and a smaller share of CPUs (central processing units). The GPU-to-CPU ratios in AI data centers built for training were recently around 8-to-1.

However, handling the workloads for agentic AI will require servers with many more CPUs. Agentic AI processes require the systems to determine all the steps needed to complete a task and execute them in order. That's a job for a CPU, not a GPU. According to experts, data centers built for agentic AI will need to have equal numbers of GPUs and CPUS, and Laffont believes Intel is well positioned to benefit as a result.

While we've already seen the huge inflection in GPU demand, this intensifying wave of CPU demand is just getting started, Coatue's analysts argue. As more tasks are handed off to agents, CPU demand will skyrocket. They see the total addressable market for server CPUs climbing from $40 billion in 2026 to $300 billion in 2031.

Of course, Intel isn't the only company competing for share in server GPUs. It faces competition from several large chipmakers, including AMD, Qualcomm, Arm Holdings, and even Nvidia. Nonetheless, it's showing strong progress capitalizing on the opportunity so far, with data center revenue climbing 78% year over year in the last quarter, even as it remains supply-constrained.

Intel holds an even larger share of the PC CPU market, which has faced challenges as a result of rising memory prices. Management expects PC unit sales to decline 20% in the second half of 2026 and another 10% in 2027. That will weigh on the company's growth until memory prices come back down, considering PC sales still account for more of Intel’s revenue than data center CPUs.

Intel's stock price has fallen quite a bit since it peaked this summer. Laffont thinks the pullback is a buying opportunity. In the second quarter, he initiated a position of over 12 million shares for Coatue, and added 3.6 million more shares last quarter. With the stock now trading well below the price it fetched over the summer, he may be in the market to buy more. And considering the massive market opportunity ahead of the company, its current valuation of about 40 times forward earnings appears to be a fair price for the stock, even as Intel faces stiff competition in data centers and headwinds in the PC market.

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

#3091. 3 Monthly Dividend Stocks to Buy in the Financial Sector

This particular industry is perfectly suited to generate recurring income.

By James Brumley – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:45AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Main Street Capital ›

Contrary to a common assumption, not every dividend stock pays its dividends quarterly. Although they're relatively rare, a handful of these income-generating equity investments pay a dividend every month, better aligning with how most investors/consumers incur their recurring living expenses.

Here's a closer look at three such monthly dividend payers. Although they're all from the financial sector and seemingly in similar businesses, each one is distinct from the other two. It wouldn't be wrong to hold a stake in all three if securing monthly dividend income is your goal right now.

Main Street Capital (MAIN -1.10%) is categorized as a business development company, or BDC. That just means (as the term suggests) it helps up-and-coming organizations grow by supplying them with capital -- and, occasionally, some degree of direction. This capital can come in the form of a loan or in exchange for equity in that enterprise. Either way, as a registered BDC, Main Street Capital qualifies for certain corporate-level tax breaks, making this business structure a cost-efficient way of tapping into young companies' potential.

You may be familiar with some of the outfits in its portfolio. Propane supplier Flame King, software company Volusion, and utility-scale radiator manufacturer Trantech are just some of the businesses that have benefited from the funding offered by Main Street Capital.

It's not an entirely consistent business. As you might imagine, the ever-changing economic backdrop pushes and pulls on its profitability, which in turn can stifle the otherwise reliable growth of its dividend payments. For instance, these payments stagnated in 2020, and in 2008 in the wake of the subprime mortgage meltdown.

Its dividends have never gone unpaid, though, nor have they ever shrunk. You'd also be plugging into a forward-looking dividend yield of just over 8%, when including its quarterly bonus dividend in addition to its regular monthly payments.

Between the two, Main Street Capital's total annual payout has improved from 2016's $2.73 per share to last fiscal year's $4.35. That's not bad at all, especially given the decent price gains this stock's mustered during the same 10-year time frame.

Like Main Street Capital, Capital Southwest (CSWC -1.54%) is a business development company, enjoying all the same tax benefits. With a forward-looking dividend yield of around 13%, however, Capital Southwest clearly does things differently than most other BDCs.

That difference -- as you might imagine -- is the risk it takes with the loans it makes. In exchange for taking on more credit risk, it requires higher interest payments, which ultimately translate into bigger dividends for shareholders. The organization's weighted average yield on its current loan portfolio is a hefty 10.9%.

The catch? Eventually, taking on too much risk can come back to haunt you —  like now. Technically, between last quarter's ordinary monthly dividends and its special dividend, on a per-share basis Capital Southwest dished out more in dividend payments than it actually earned. Per-share profits also fell year over year despite the increase in net investment income (a BDC's equivalent of revenue).

That's a contributing reason why this ticker hasn't performed particularly well for the past few years, while the economic and lending environment has been hit-and-miss.

It's not catastrophic. The company was still able to cover most of last quarter's dividend payment with actual earnings, as it typically does. Once interest rates and the economy stabilize, look for this BDC to once again fully fund its regular monthly dividend as well as the additional performance-based quarterly kicker.

In the meantime, take advantage of this ticker's 10% tumble from August's peak, reflecting concerns that Capital Southwest's more aggressive lending policy isn't safe enough for this economic environment.

This organization's approach is more resilient than the market is giving it credit for, allowing you to plug into it while its yield is elevated. Just keep in mind that while the dividend yield here is phenomenal, the dividend payment barely grows from one year to the next. That's the trade-off.

Last but not least, add Trinity Capital (TRIN -1.66%) to your list of the financial sector's monthly dividend payers to consider buying into at this time.

Yes, it's yet another business development company, and more like Capital Southwest than Main Street Capital. Its forward-looking dividend yield of nearly 12% reflects the above-average risk of its $2.5 billion loan and financing portfolio, with an effective interest yield of just over 15%.

However, Trinity is different enough from Capital Southwest in a couple of key ways that owning both might still make sense. The first of these differences is where Trinity Capital's borrowers are located. Although the BDC works with plenty of domestic enterprises, it's willing and able to deploy capital overseas.

The second of these key differences is that Trinity is more likely to exit an equity stake and move on to another opportunity than most other business development companies are. While all of them do it to some degree (out of necessity), this $1.7 billion organization sold $237 million worth of its equity investments and collected $194 million in early debt repayments last quarter alone.

This pace of turnover isn't necessarily good or bad. It's just different, underscoring how -- compared to most other business development companies -- Trinity Capital is more heavily focused on equity than on lending. This adds some diversity to whatever arrangement of monthly dividend payers you're eyeing.

With that being said, you should know that Trinity hasn't raised its annualized dividend since 2024. This doesn't mean it will never happen again. It just means you can't count on it every year, if you know you need it.

Even so, with such a high yield at the same time this ticker's moved measurably higher since this bull market took hold in 2023, a stagnant monthly dividend payment may still be worth it.

#3089. Red Cat Holdings: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its nearly $243 million cash pile is meant to fund the push into autonomous aerial and maritime defense, but the question is whether that bet can pay off.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:52AM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, Red Cat Holdings (RCAT -7.47%) announced that it withdrew its full-year 2026 revenue target. Delays in defense contract awards pushed expected customer orders past prior timelines.

The business holds $242.7 million in cash to fund its long-term expansion into autonomous aerial and maritime defense platforms. Three statements from management capture the key takeaways for long-term investors.

Management pulled its revenue outlook after FANG, the company's first-person view drone, missed selection as a finalist in the military's Drone Dominance II competition. Deferred military spending schedules also delayed anticipated customer deliveries across several defense programs.

To avoid shipping delays when defense orders materialize, Red Cat built up $127 million in inventory and prepaid inventory by the end of the third quarter. Management designed this stock of key components to support immediate fulfillment for military buyers.

The company combined its Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace drone subsidiaries into Red Cat Aerial, an integrated division for military aerial systems. The consolidation eliminated overlapping operational roles and reduced corporate headcount.

Demand for uncrewed defense systems is expanding across global military markets. A 155,000-square-foot production plant in Georgia and its impending acquisition of a power systems maker provide manufacturing infrastructure. Management is watching contract conversions and production efficiency to improve margins as orders ramp.

Commercializing integrated aerial and maritime platforms remains central to long-term growth as defense clients scale up autonomous technology deployment.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

Atmos Rewards offers six communities, each with its own travel perks and opportunities to earn bonus points

Atmos Rewards is the airline loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. One of its newer features is Atmos Communities, which offer additional rewards and benefits tailored to different travel interests.

There are six communities, including two reserved for Alaska and Hawaii residents. The other four are open to members regardless of where they live. But don’t get caught up in the community names. The best choice for you may depend more on your travel plans than the groupings suggest.

Here’s how to decide which Atmos Community best fits your travel patterns.

Atmos Communities are like groups within the Atmos Rewards program that offer additional benefits based on different travel interests.

They’re free to join for Atmos Rewards members. Four communities are available to all members, while community Club 49 is reserved for Alaska residents and community Huaka’i by Hawaiian is reserved for Hawaii residents.

You can belong to only one community at a time and switch communities once per calendar year. Consider your upcoming travel plans before choosing.

Joining a community is easy: Log in to your Atmos Rewards account and navigate to “Account overview.” Select “Join a Community,” browse the options and click the “Join” button under the one you choose.

Each Atmos Community has a list of 10 destinations where members can earn bonus points and status points. Although the destinations differ by community, the rewards structure is the same.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, members can earn up to 10,000 bonus points and 10,000 status points by visiting qualifying destinations.

Here’s how many points you’ll earn as you reach each milestone:

Visit one destination, earn 100 status and bonus points.

Visit two destinations, earn 200 status and bonus points.

Visit three destinations, earn 300 status and bonus points.

Visit four destinations, earn 400 status and bonus points.

Visit five destinations, earn 500 status and bonus points.

Visit six destinations, earn 750 status and bonus points.

Visit seven destinations, earn 1,000 status and bonus points.

Visit eight destinations, earn 1,250 status and bonus points.

Visit nine destinations, earn 2,500 status and bonus points.

Visit 10 destinations, earn 3,000 status and bonus points.

The first member of each community to visit all 10 qualifying destinations during the challenge period will also earn 100,000 bonus points.

New lists of qualifying destinations for each community take effect on Jan. 1, 2028.

Here’s a closer look at the six communities, their benefits and the destinations eligible for bonus points.

Global Locals is geared toward frequent international travelers. Benefits include:

Earn 10% more status points toward Atmos elite status on flights that begin and/or end outside the U.S., including award flights.

Earn 1 status point for every 25 points transferred to Atmos Rewards from Bilt or Marriott Bonvoy.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these 10 Oneworld Alliance hubs count toward bonus points and status points. Qualifying layovers also count toward the destination challenge, so you don’t necessarily need to make these cities your final stop.

If you frequently travel internationally or have any upcoming flights through any of these airports, including qualifying layovers, Global Locals might be a fit for you.

If you have the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, you’ll earn 3 Atmos points per $1 spent on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, dining and foreign transactions. The last bonus category can be especially useful for frequent international travelers.

This community has a similar setup to Global Locals, but most of its bonus destinations are in the U.S. Here’s what you can get:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

This community would be an excellent choice if your upcoming travels include several of these airports, even if dining isn't the main reason for your trips. If dining out is one of your favorite activities, check out the best credit cards for restaurants.

Active Escapes focuses on airports in outdoor-oriented destinations that are all in the U.S., save one. Benefits here are:

While these airports are gateways to national parks and other natural attractions, you don’t have to be an outdoor enthusiast to benefit. Like before, don’t let the heading sway you. Rather, consider the destinations before you decide.

Families On the Go might appeal to you if you redeem Atmos Rewards for your children. Benefits include:

Get 20% of your points back on eligible award flights for kids 12 and under after you complete your trip.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

This community may be especially valuable if you regularly book award flights for children 12 and under. Even if you don't travel with kids, it could be worth considering if its qualifying airports align better with your travel plans than those of other communities.

Exclusively for Alaska residents, Club 49 offers rewards that are focused on travel to, from and within the state:

Two free checked bags when traveling to or from Alaska on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines.

#3082. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

Legacy low-margin contracts are rolling off, and management expects that drag to stop being a talking point after FY '27.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 21, 2026 at 11:53AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Mercury Systems ›

On its first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Mercury (MRCY -6.61%) raised its full-year revenue outlook. The defense-processing hardware provider is shifting low-margin development contracts to higher-volume production orders. Three things management said stand out.

As development programs complete, customer orders are shifting into higher-volume manufacturing. This transition expanded total backlog--the value of contracted orders awaiting fulfillment--past $2 billion and boosted first-quarter bookings by 48% year over year.

For quarters, low-margin legacy development work dragged on profitability. Management is burning down that legacy backlog and replacing it with production orders aligned with its target profile for adjusted EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization.

Mercury paid down $250 million in debt over two quarters, including a $100 million payment against its revolving credit facility in Q1. Lower debt gives the company balance sheet flexibility to fund internal growth.

Operations across manufacturing facilities are gaining momentum as material availability improves and factory capacity remains underutilized at single-shift levels. Management is watching program execution, pricing discipline, and supply chain lead times as defense spending flows into firm orders.

Long-term value creation depends on converting high-volume defense production into steady cash flow while maintaining operating cost discipline.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased today, but borrowing costs are still expensive for many home buyers.

Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a big reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.74% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3072. Is IonQ Stock a Buy Right Now?

IonQ has a long way to go before becoming a viable company.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 21, 2026 at 12:00PM EST

IonQ (IONQ -8.76%) is an intriguing stock. It hasn't done well in 2026 and is down nearly 50% this year and down around 70% from its all-time high. On the surface, that doesn't look promising. However, once investors wrap their heads around what is going on, it starts to look much more inviting.

IonQ is the biggest pure-play quantum computing investment available on the market, and its business continues to grow rapidly as demand for early-stage quantum computers arrives. But with the market seemingly not caring about this growth, the stock is cheap.

So, is now the perfect time to buy? I think so, as the market could care less about quantum computing right now.

IonQ is a pure-play quantum computing company, meaning it doesn't have any other businesses to fund its operations. So, it must produce a viable quantum computer or risk going bankrupt. That's a high-risk scenario, but the rewards will be immense if IonQ can pull it off.

The market selling off IonQ's stock during 2026 has little to do with how it's actually doing as a company. Instead, it is more of a reflection of the market's risk appetite. Investors have gotten wary of investing in higher-risk investments during 2026. AI is generally considered a lower risk than quantum computing because there's actually usable technology in that sector. So, with quantum computing being an even riskier segment than that, the market has heavily sold it off.

However, I think that makes the timing right to buy IonQ stock, as the time to buy is when there is no fanfare around the industry.

IonQ has been making great strides toward becoming a viable business. Next year, its 256-qubit Superion system launches, which will be one of the most powerful early-stage quantum computers available. It has several clients that have already preordered, and with $1.2 billion in revenue backlog, there is monster demand for this product.

However, IonQ isn't just focused on developing a viable quantum computer. Earlier this year, it acquired SkyWater, which is a semiconductor foundry. This helps decrease development time for IonQ and also gives it more control over its supply chain.

It also acquired Elisity, which will help IonQ pioneer quantum-focused cybersecurity. All of these moves were made to make IonQ a one-stop shop for all things quantum computing-related. It is a bold strategy and could turn it into the next tech giant if it works out, but there's no guarantee of success.

Investors must understand and manage risk with IonQ, as it is far from a surefire investment.

IonQ isn't the only company competing in this space. There are countless others, including several well-funded big tech companies. IonQ is also taking a different technological approach that prioritizes accuracy over computing speed. This may be an advantage in the early stages of quantum computing, as accuracy is one of the primary concerns for users. But if companies with faster processing speeds catch up to IonQ's accuracy levels, then IonQ could be in trouble.

The question of whether IonQ turns into a successful company pivots around how quickly it can launch its commercially viable quantum computer and how much of a head start (if any) it has on its competitors. That will determine the investing success of IonQ, and there's no way of knowing for sure if it will even reach the commercially viable state.

As a result, if you're going to invest in IonQ, then keeping position sizing small (say 1%) is a smart idea. I think IonQ is an excellent long-shot investment opportunity, but only if you have the mindset that this stock is more of a lottery ticket right now.

#3068. Eli Lilly's Next Big Growth Opportunity Could Be Hiding in Plain Sight

Lilly’s famous weight-loss drug may be about to get younger.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 21, 2026 at 12:17PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Eli Lilly ›

Eli Lilly (LLY -0.30%) delivered yet another impressive earnings report last month. The company's third-quarter update showed that its core growth drivers, including Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for weight loss, don't seem anywhere close to running out of steam. The best part is that Eli Lilly is actively looking to tap into new market niches, and some of the company's recent clinical trial results could open another important opportunity. Let's look into it.

Zepbound is currently approved for weight loss for adults aged 18 and older, provided their BMI (Body Mass Index) is at least 30 or at least 27 with a weight-related comorbidity. It isn't indicated for anyone younger than that. But Eli Lilly has been running clinical studies to test whether Zepbound is effective in younger patients. It recently reported results from one of those trials.

The study in question enrolled people aged 12 to 17. Half of them had obesity-related complications, while 75% met the threshold for class 2 or class 3 severe obesity. During the study, participants who received Zepbound lost an average of about 40 pounds, while those receiving a placebo gained an average of 5 pounds after 72 weeks.

Also, BMI decreased by 18.5% in patients who took Zepbound, compared with a 0.5% increase in the placebo group. Further, Zepbound led to improvements in various measures, including LDL cholesterol and triglycerides (which are linked to increased cardiovascular risk), as well as improved quality of life.

Safety data were consistent with what we know about GLP-1 drugs. These results could help support a label expansion for Zepbound in younger patients.

There are about 25.6 million people between 12 and 17 years of age in the U.S. The prevalence of obesity among people aged 2 to 19 has been about 21% in recent years, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Applying that to the 12- to 17-year-old population, we get a potential market of more than five million patients -- a significant opportunity.

And that's only in the U.S. Assuming Eli Lilly can generate about $6,000 in net revenue per patient and the pharmaceutical company reaches 20% penetration in this population, we are talking about an additional annual net revenue of about $6.5 billion.

Note that in the third quarter, Zepbound generated $5.4 billion in revenue, up 49% year over year. Eli Lilly's total revenue grew 39% year over year to $24.4 billion. An additional $6.5 billion in annual sales from Zepbound would therefore be meaningful. Of course, there are important caveats to consider.

For one, it will take time for Eli Lilly to ramp up Zepbound sales in this niche. Also, Eli Lilly will face competition in this market. The company's biggest challenger, Novo Nordisk (NVO -2.70%), has earned approval for its famous GLP-1 drug, Wegovy, in this patient population.

Third, Eli Lilly's net realized prices might decline as more weight loss drugs enter the market. Even with these caveats, this opportunity looks potentially highly lucrative for Eli Lilly. The company has proven that Zepbound is more effective than Wegovy. And given the benefits Zepbound demonstrated in adolescents beyond weight loss, it should attract a significant share of that market, even with increased competition. However, does this make Eli Lilly stock a buy?

The potential label expansion for Zepbound in adolescents appears attractive, and it once again highlights Eli Lilly's strength in one of its core therapeutic areas. Eli Lilly is also running clinical trials for Zepbound in patients between six and 11 years of age, which could add more than five million patients to its addressable market, provided the medicine proves effective in this study.

And we haven't even mentioned the several other clinical trial candidates the company has in weight loss or, for that matter, the deep pipeline it has built in other therapeutic areas, such as oncology. So, Eli Lilly's prospects look attractive. The stock has outperformed broader equities this year -- and since the turn of the decade, for that matter -- but there may be plenty of upside left.
