#3065. College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

#3063. Here's How Many Shares of Coca-Cola You'd Need for $1,000 in Monthly Income

Just like Berkshire Hathaway, you can build a steady income stream with Coca-Cola stock.

By Thomas Niel – Nov 21, 2026 at 12:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Coca-Cola ›

With 64 years of consecutive dividend increases, Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) is one of the Dividend Kings, if not one of the quintessential blue chip dividend stocks. This dividend growth and dependability are likely major factors behind the stock's continued presence in Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio.

Berkshire's 400 million-share position, worth around $39.6 billion, generates nearly $850 million in annual dividend income. Investors operating on a smaller scale could make it a core holding to build their own steady income stream.

Coca-Cola currently pays a $0.53-per-share cash dividend, equating to $2.12 in annual dividends per share. To generate $1,000 per month, or $12,000 per year, divide $12,000 by $2.12. This gives you around 5,661 shares.

With Coca-Cola recently trading at around $99 per share, you would need to invest $560,439 to generate $12,001.32 in annual dividend income. This works out to a dividend yield of around 2.15%. At a time when the federal funds rate stands at nearly 3.9%, this may not sound significant, but consider the other benefits of buying and holding Coca-Cola over the long term.

Over the past decade, dividend increases have averaged 4.45% annually. If this trend continues and Coca-Cola keeps raising its dividend by 4% to 5% per year, a decade from now, this same position could be generating between $1,480 and $1,628 per month in dividend income.

Although Coca-Cola has trailed the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) in total returns over the last decade, the stock has outperformed the market index in more recent years, particularly over the past year. That's not to say that this trend will continue. After this recent hot streak, for instance, Coca-Cola shares have reached a relatively high valuation of 28.5 times forward earnings. While it may be a stronger buy on a pullback, its dividend durability and growth still make it a solid core position in a long-term income-focused portfolio.

#3056. Warren Buffett Said Stocks Are Better Than Bonds for Long-Term Investors. History Shows He Was Right.

A bad experience with Treasury bonds made Warren Buffett even more of a believer in stocks for the long run. See why.

By Ben Gran – Nov 21, 2026 at 12:45PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF ›

Warren Buffett became a legendary investor by investing in stocks, not bonds. But he had some strong opinions about bonds that other investors should consider.

Many people think of bonds as being "less risky" than stocks, and that can be true. But understanding the "risk" of bonds vs. stocks depends on your time horizon and investment goals.

In his 2017 shareholder letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, Warren Buffett shared an interesting story about his experience with the true risks of bonds. This experience reminded him why he prefers buying stocks.

Let's look at why Buffett said that stocks are a better buy than bonds for most long-term investors.

In 2017, Buffett was reaching the end of a unique, public 10-year-long wager. He had made a friendly bet with an investment advisory firm, Protégé Partners, to see if professional hedge fund managers could outperform the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) for the next 10 years, starting in 2008.

Buffett bet that they couldn't. He believed that most professional money managers would fail to beat the S&P 500 for that long.

Buffett was right. All five of the professional hedge fund managers chosen by Protégé failed to beat the S&P 500.

The bet involved $1 million, with Buffett and Protégé each pledging $500,000 toward that total. No matter who won the bet, the $1 million proceeds would go to a Nebraska charity, Girls Inc. of Omaha.

To fund the bet, Buffett and Protégé each bought a package of zero-coupon U.S. Treasury bonds worth $318,250 when purchased at the start of the bet (about 64% of face value) and would be worth $500,000 after 10 years (for a total of $1 million at the end of the bet).

But midway through the bet, in 2012, Buffett realized that due to recent changes in the bond market, their zero-coupon Treasury bonds had become a terrible investment. The bonds had started out yielding about 4.56% annually, but by 2012, with five years left until maturity, they were yielding only about 0.88% annually.

Warren Buffett can't abide a bad deal on an investment. He and Protégé quickly agreed to sell their Treasury bonds and put the proceeds into Berkshire Hathaway (BRKB -0.36%) Class B shares. He was confident that Berkshire Hathaway stock would deliver a much better average annual return for the next five years than 0.88%.

Once again, he was right. As a result, as Buffett wrote: "Girls Inc. of Omaha found itself receiving $2,222,279 last month rather than the $1 million it had originally hoped for."

Buffett's experience with Treasury bonds taught a few important lessons about the real risks of bond investing. Here are a few reasons, according to Buffett, why bonds can be riskier than stocks:

Buffett wrote that investing is about giving up consumption today so you can have more money to spend later. But bonds can fail to achieve this goal if they don't make your money grow in the long run.

As he wrote, "By that standard, purportedly 'risk-free' long-term bonds in 2012 were a far riskier investment than a long-term investment in common stocks."

If inflation is 3% per year and bonds deliver 4% yields, they're barely staying ahead of inflation. Buffett bought those zero-coupon Treasury bonds at a time of lower inflation and lower interest rates than we have today. But from 2012 to 2017, his bonds were on track to yield only 0.88% per year.

Buffett noted this inflation risk of bonds when he wrote: "At that time, even a 1% annual rate of inflation between 2012 and 2017 would have decreased the purchasing-power of the government bond that Protégé and I sold."

The S&P 500 can crash on any given day, but it tends to go up in the long run. That means the longer your time horizon, the longer you can hold your stocks, and the more likely they’ll deliver a positive return. Bonds can be safer than stocks in the short run, but over time, stocks gradually become a better bet.

As Buffett wrote: "...in any upcoming day, week, or even year, stocks will be riskier -- far riskier -- than short-term U.S. bonds. As an investor's investment horizon lengthens, however, a diversified portfolio of U.S. equities becomes progressively less risky than bonds, assuming that the stocks are purchased at a sensible multiple of earnings relative to then-prevailing interest rates."

Buffett followed up on these ideas in his shareholder letter in a February 2018 interview with CNBC, where he said he believed long-term investors should buy stocks rather than bonds. He said, "If you had to choose between buying long-term bonds or equities, I would choose equities in a minute...If I were going to own a 30-year government bond or own equities for 30 years, I think equities will considerably outperform that 30-year bond."

History shows that Warren Buffett was right. In the eight years since Buffett's shareholder letter and CNBC interview in Feb. 2018, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%) has strongly outperformed the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF (BND +0.59%).

This doesn't mean you shouldn't buy any bonds. Bond ETFs can be appropriate as part of a diversified portfolio. Today's bonds offer higher yields than they did when Buffett was buying Treasury bonds in 2008, which could make them a better deal for investors than they used to be. I own shares of the Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF, even though my time horizon for investing is still decades long.

But if you want maximum growth of your money and can hold for the long term through short-term stock market booms and busts, buying stocks should be the foundation of your investment strategy.

Trailing-12-month free cash flow (FCF) of $4.9 billion accounted for 35% of revenue, which is a superb margin. The board of directors had the confidence to approve a $12 billion buyback, in addition to the $2.7 billion in existing capacity.

The growth stock has had a wonderful year. It's up 33% in 2026 (as of Nov. 18). Here's what that share repurchase runway means for investors.

Airbnb is known for having sizable stock-based compensation, totaling $1.4 billion over the last nine months. This is how businesses, particularly those earlier in their life cycles, pay their employees. But it results in an increase in the share count.

To Airbnb's credit, though, its outstanding share count shrank by almost 3% in the past year. The company conducted $4 billion in stock buybacks over the last 12 months. Combining the new $12 billion repurchase authorization with the $2.7 billion remaining capacity means Airbnb now intends to buy 12% of the company's entire market capitalization.

Investors benefit from this tailwind. A smaller outstanding share count provides a jolt to earnings per share (EPS). Shareholders who continue to hold the stock see their ownership percentage in the business increase over time.

The best companies can balance returning capital to investors with reinvesting into their operations. Airbnb is certainly still playing offense.

The business continues to expand its list of services. Travelers can now book hotels. And there are more active partnerships in place. And for hosts, a redesigned calendar makes juggling multiple listings far simpler.

Airbnb is also leaning into the opportunity that artificial intelligence (AI) presents. It plans to release an AI-powered travel assistant in 2027.

For context, in fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 26), Apple (AAPL -1.90%) produced $136.1 billion in FCF, a mind-boggling figure. Its FCF margin was 28%, however, which is lower than Airbnb’s FCF margin.

Hats off to Airbnb's asset-light business model. The company doesn't own the properties listed on its platform, eliminating the need for a sizable investment. And that frees up cash for repurchasing shares.

This leads to the next point, which concerns the wide economic moat Airbnb has built since its founding in 2007. The company benefits from a powerful global network effect. It's a positive feedback loop in which more guest bookings attract more hosts to try to make money from their listings. In turn, the wider selection leads to a better, more compelling experience for travelers.

The fear that AI agents will handle the entire booking process for consumers and challenge this favorable position is warranted. However, Airbnb's advantage as the middleman comes from convenience, trust, and centralized tools it offers to both guests and hosts. The strong Q3 financial figures prove there is no cause for alarm yet.

"As we build Airbnb to become an AI-native company, I actually think the opportunity ahead of us is actually even bigger," co-founder and chief executive officer Brian Chesky said on the Q3 2026 earnings call.

Airbnb is worth keeping an eye on, provided you're an investor searching for high-quality stocks to own for five years or more. It's a compounding machine. Consensus analyst estimates call for EPS to grow at an annualized rate of 24% from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2028.

Because shares trade at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 29.7, much of the good news is already reflected. Know this before you make a move.

#3040. If the Fed Hikes Rates This Year, I'm Loading Up on This 1 ETF

The Vanguard Energy ETF could be an even bigger sector exchange-traded fund star if the Fed raises interest rates again.

By Todd Shriber – Nov 21, 2026 at 1:08PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Energy ETF ›

With just three weeks left before the Federal Reserve's December meeting, it's basically a foregone conclusion that the central bank will raise interest rates for a second time this year.

Speaking of interest rates, investors preparing for 2027 should note that Goldman Sachs recently forecast one more rate hike by the Fed next March, before the central bank begins to cut rates later in the year. We don’t know what the future holds, but the point is, it's nearly a sure thing that at least one more rate increase is on the way and more can't be ruled out.

Federal Reserve headquarters in Washington, D.C. Image source: Getty Images.

So now is an excellent time for equity investors of all stripes to understand that Fed actions affect various sectors in different ways. For example, the capital-intensive, debt-heavy utility sector is often vulnerable to higher borrowing costs when rates rise. In contrast, higher rates are seen as boons to financial services stocks due to net interest margin expansion.

Energy stocks have also shown strength as rates rise, suggesting that exchange-traded funds (ETFs) such as the Vanguard Energy ETF (VDE -0.73%) are worth considering ahead of the next Fed meeting and beyond.

Home to the largest domestic energy companies, the $11.9 billion Vanguard Energy ETF is one of this year's stars among basic sector ETFs, as highlighted by a year-to-date gain of 43% as I write this.

There's no denying that energy ETFs, including this Vanguard fund, are getting big boosts from oil prices driven up by current wars, but energy stocks also have a track record of performing well when interest rates rise. The Fed — whose main role is to promote “maximum employment” and “stable prices” — has already raised rates once this year, and 10- and 30-year Treasury yields recently touched their highest levels since 2002.

The bottom line is that energy stocks and ETFs such as this Vanguard fund are doing their jobs in a challenging interest rate environment, providing investors with effective portfolio hedges while stocks and bonds falter.

So it's pretty safe to say that we're in for at least one more rate hike, if not two, in the short term, but that doesn't make this Vanguard ETF a risk-free bet heading into 2027. Oil prices are notoriously volatile, and if new Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress succeed in compelling President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran, oil prices would likely tumble, potentially taking energy ETFs along for the ride.

Additionally, this ETF is top-heavy. It allocates nearly 40% of its weight to ExxonMobil (XOM +0.67%) and Chevron (CVX +0.91%). Those stocks have been sturdy this year, but if one sneezes, it's possible, if not probable, the other does the same, and this Vanguard ETF catches a cold.

Of course, there are no guarantees that any of those scenarios come to pass. I'm just laying out possible risks for investors evaluating this ETF.

There are plenty of bright spots to ponder, too. For example, Exxon and Chevron have strong balance sheets and are two of the energy patch's most dependable dividend growers. And in broader terms, the global energy sector is sporting the best earnings momentum of any sector over the past several months. On that basis, energy is even beating technology, and by a healthy margin at that. If that strength continues into 2027, the Vanguard Energy ETF won't need rising rates to thrive, but investors will certainly accept that assistance. And if the Fed raises rates this year, I plan to buy shares.

#3035. Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Right Now?

The company is going through a very difficult time.

By Will Ebiefung – Nov 21, 2026 at 1:15PM EST

November has been absolutely terrible for Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%). A series of scandals has led to the removal of its CEO and founder, Jensen Huang. Widespread uncertainty about the company's future has caused shares to drop nearly 30% since the start of the month.

This is all happening against the backdrop of a generative artificial intelligence (AI) industry that many fear could be a bubble that is soon to be popped by changing regulation and investor appetite for risk. Let's dig deeper into the pros and cons of Nvidia to decide what might come next.

Nvidia's current crisis began on Oct. 29, when The New York Times reported that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was a possible target of an espionage plot. The suspicions centered around his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at one of Nvidia's major clients, the Singapore-based Megaspeed. Jensen Huang was also involved in potential misconduct related to his relationships with Nvidia employees. On Nov. 12, he resigned amid a board investigation expected to lead to his termination.

These developments led to a sharp decline in Nvidia's stock price, and it isn't hard to see why. For starters, the espionage allegations will cast a dark shadow over Nvidia's entire Asian operation. Buyers in countries like Singapore and Malaysia could be used to reroute Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, bypassing U.S. sanctions.

There may even be unwanted regulatory scrutiny of Nvidia's past business dealings with China-affiliated clients. Huang is expected to eventually testify before U.S. lawmakers concerning this issue.

However, beyond the tangible business effects, Nvidia may now face an even bigger problem: the loss of its founder's vision. Huang's leadership was instrumental in helping turn Nvidia from just another Silicon Valley hardware producer into the world's largest chipmaker. It is unclear if a new CEO will have the same vision and tenacity. According to Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, the company could lose up to 30% of its value without Huang at the helm. That's bad news for investors.

The good news is that Nvidia's chip business is still firing on all cylinders. Third-quarter earnings were a slam dunk, with revenue jumping 103% year over year to $115.8 billion. This result was driven by ravenous demand from data center clients, which use Nvidia's hardware to run and train large language models (LLMs) and other AI-related use cases.

The soaring growth is expected to continue over the next few quarters, as AI-related spending shows no sign of slowing any time soon. S&P Global expects America's largest hyperscalers to spend $1.3 trillion on AI infrastructure next year. Much of that capital will likely flow into Nvidia's products because of their cutting-edge design and capabilities.

That said, Nvidia's data center segment now represents 93% of its revenue, making the company exceptionally vulnerable to a drop in data center demand.

The market could weaken because of regulatory changes. Many Democratic lawmakers are already pledging to push back on data center construction. Rising interest rates could also pose a problem, as they make it more expensive for clients to raise the debt capital needed to purchase large volumes of chips. There is also the risk that demand on the customer-facing side of the AI industry will not be sufficient to justify the substantial spending on AI infrastructure.

While Nvidia's recent dip might make the stock look like a tempting buy right now, the risks seem to outweigh the rewards. The recent scandal could expose Nvidia to heightened regulatory scrutiny of its business in Asia. The loss of Huang's leadership could hurt the company in ways that are difficult to predict right now. Investors should stay on the sidelines until more information becomes available.
